#6189. Over Arepas and Cachitos, Venezuelans in Madrid Find a Sense of Home

I stroll down the wide aisles of the sprawling Mercado de Las Maravillas, passing greengrocers with yuca and plantains piled high. A digital billboard flashes congratulations for the recent Venezuelan team’s World Baseball Classic win. Nearby, a vendor hawks yellow, blue, and red flags, while signs advertising remittance services to Latin America clutter my sightline. All around me, the Madrid market fills with the round, sing-song accent of Venezuelan Spanish.

I make my way to the prepared-food stalls aisle, where the woman at Buda Bar Delicias Venezolanas draws me in by calling me amor and asking what I’d like to order, reina. The familiar warmth of Latin America—I lived in Mexico before moving to Spain—tears open a pang of nostalgia in my chest. Guests seated at the stainless-steel bar munch on empanadas de carne mechada, continuously reaching for the green, herby salsa guasacaca. “How can it be that they are pumping a million barrels of oil out a day but they cannot fix a single hospital in Caracas?” I overhear another diner say to a friend, discussing the latest spate of frustrations back home.

The Mercado de Las Maravillas is "where the Venezolanismo here in Madrid started,” restaurant owner Manuel Pérez Álvarez says.

Among Madrid’s 130,000-strong Venezuelan diaspora, these conversations are not uncommon. Spain’s Venezuelan population has swollen to almost 700,000 people, making it the largest community outside of the Americas, and a significant portion of the country’s nearly eight million citizens living abroad. Many have fled their homeland amid the economic and political instability that followed Hugo Chavez’s Bolivarian Revolution and continued under Nicolás Maduro’s rule. Ongoing uncertainty continues to drive migration. Unlike other diasporas, Madrid’s Venezuelan population isn’t concentrated in a single neighborhood. Instead, it stretches across the city and spans a broad socioeconomic spectrum, from delivery drivers and financiers to political exiles.

Its food institutions mirror a similar range.

Manuel Pérez Álvarez and his wife Maira María Gómez can pinpoint the moment they decided to open a Venezuelan restaurant in Madrid. The two, who moved to Spain in 1997 after a lifetime in the coastal city of Puerto de La Cruz, had gone to meet friends for Venezuelan empanadas at one of the few spots in town at the time. After waiting 45 minutes for their order in a long line of people hankering for a taste of home, Pérez—a natural entrepreneur—saw opportunity.

Manuel Pérez Álvarez and his wife Maira María Gómez opened El Empanadazo in Madrid nearly a decade ago.

Venezuela's national dish, pabellon criollo—rice, beans, shredded beef, and plantains—is served alongside cachapas, arepas, fried fish, and more.

When they opened El Empanadazo nearly a decade ago, the couple joined the ranks of just a handful of other Venezuelan food joints. They chose to set up shop in the Mercado de Las Maravillas. “It was really where the Venezolanismo here in Madrid started,” Pérez says of the market. In no time, they were serving hearty plates of Venezuela's national dish, pabellon criollo—rice, beans, shredded beef, and plantains—crispy fried whole fish, sweet corn griddled cachapas, arepas, and more.

“Our restaurant really became a gathering place for Venezuelans. I remember the early days when I was spending more time there, seeing people with tears in their eyes,” Pérez says. “When you’re an immigrant, little things like the taste of home really get to you.”

Maira María Gómez and her husband Manuel Pérez Álvarez opened El Empanadazo in Madrid nearly a decade ago, there were far fewer Venezuelan restaurants in the city.

At the time, Venezuelan food wasn’t as easy to find and people went out of their way for it. Today, a quick search for “arepa” on the delivery apps will turn up hundreds of options. “Now there are lots of spots, but we were really pioneers, and it wasn’t even all that long ago,” Pérez says.

Be it Arepa’s Coffee Shop nestled next to the hustle of the Moncloa train and bus station, or the four-location La Arepera, the Insta-famous El Chino Venezolano, or the fast-growing Guasacaca, the country’s gastronomic footprint continues to grow alongside its diaspora in Madrid. At the March 2026 Arepa Fest, a celebration of Venezuelan and Colombian food and culture, in the north edges of Madrid, more than 5,000 people gathered to snack on the region's signature split- and stuffed-cornmeal snack, while the sound system alternated between pumping Venezuelan Merengue and reggaeton.

At Panadería Torrerí, warm pastries like cachitos, a brioche-like crescent roll most typically filled with ham and cheese, and golfeados, spiral pastry dough filled with cheese, keep customers coming back.

A similar fervor can be felt at Panadería Torrerí. By mid-morning, the team is already replenishing their glass case of cachitos, a brioche-like crescent roll most typically filled with ham and cheese, and golfeados, spiral pastry dough filled with cheese, and brushed with panela (unrefined cane sugar) and anise. Regulars grab a table and owner Mara Azuaje, always poised with a “¿Cómo está usted?” quickly ferries over their order.

Azuaje opened her bakery in 2024 to bring traditional Venezuelan pastries to the neighborhood of Barrio de Salamanca. For years, there had been no Venezuelan bakery in the area, despite this upscale neighborhood being nicknamed “Little Caracas” for its substantial diaspora. Today, Panadería Torrerí attracts both affluent property owners alongside motorbike messengers, all looking for a taste of home.

Mara Azuaje opened Panadería Torrerí in the Barrio de Salamanca in 2024.

Azuaje, who came to Spain at 27, knows what they're after. She spent years working odd jobs to save the money needed to open her bakery. “I cleaned homes, worked as a delivery driver, took care of children. I did whatever, but I was always very ambitious,” Azuaje says. “I wanted to have my own business.”

She didn’t understand the exact shape it would take, but her grandmother’s lessons to her as a child around the importance of learning an oficio, a craft, stayed with her. “I was always baking with my grandmother who told me I needed to know how to do something, so I opened a bakery,” she says. Today, Azuaje is proud to be known across the neighborhood for her homemade bread and her hearty rolled-dough pastries.

Other Venezuelan restaurant owners transitioned into hospitality later in life. At Bea Castelló Castro and Luis Felipe Fossa’s Cafetín, the menu—arepas with chia seeds, shredded chicken, and avocado for breakfast, or creamed curry soup and sweet corn and hearty salads for lunch—carries traces of Venezuela while honoring the other places the couple has called home.

At Cafetín, the menu showcases Venezuelan flavors through a global lens.

Cafetín's arepas are stuffed with chia seeds, shredded chicken, and avocado

The married pair came to Madrid after a full life in Caracas. “By 2007 Chávez just kept winning and winning, and things were getting worse and worse. It really scared us,” Felipe says. That year was Chávez’s first attempt at constitutional reform to remove presidential term limits and expand state control of the economy. He lost his bid but remained in power and went on to secure reform in 2009. So, when the bank Fossa worked for offered him a job in Zurich, they didn’t hesitate. It was a decision that has led to many years of living abroad.

Bea Castelló Castro and Luis Felipe Fossa say that their Cafetín has become a hub for Venezuelans, who connect over coffee and arepas.

Their clientele reflects a similar worldliness, with Venezuelans who arrived directly from Caracas but also those who have made it here by way of a university in Boston, or lived for years in Miami, New York, or London. Cafetín is a meeting point where these Venezuelans intersect, creating a community within a community. As Castelló Castro put it, “empiezas a hacer nexo”—you start to make connections.

Recently, I'm told, a couple in a sunlit corner of the cafe started chatting with a man standing at the long bar after hearing him mention Caracas. They began tracing the routes through Miami and New York that had brought them to Madrid. Another day, a college sweatshirt prompted a conversation—and a new friendship. “It’s beautiful to see, especially in difficult moments in Venezuela,” says Castelló Castro.

Back at the Mercado de Las Maravillas, I sit at Buda Bar watching the lunch rush fade, as owner Rebeksa Mouzaber prepares me a sweet-corn crescent-shaped cachapa, its edges lacy from a bed of hot butter on the flattop griddle. A food courier accepts a freshly-made pocket-sized empanada while he scrolls and waits for his order.

Venezuelans like coming here because they feel at home—not just in the dishes that are served but also in the way they are asked for, Mouzaber tells me. “We know what it means when they ask for an ñapa (a top-up), just like we know how it feels to be so far away from home.”

#6188. In Iceland, Ali Wong Listened to Björk’s Jazz Album and Covered Herself in Silica

“I was on tour in June and July for my new stand-up hour and managed to escape the crazy heat wave in Europe when I performed in Reykjavík, Iceland. It was my first time there, so it was quite exotic to experience the cold in July. (I live in LA, where it feels like it's getting hotter every summer.) There is a crispness that is so unique. I was with my family—my kids and my baby daddy—and Sheng Wang, who was opening all my shows. The landscape is so breathtaking. Just driving by geysers bursting and steaming out of the ground felt like witnessing magic. Whenever I travel my favorite thing is going to the biggest supermarket and buying any local snacks you can't get anywhere else. Our tour guide, Aron Karlsson, had taken us to the Bónus grocery store, where we got a ton of fish jerky and black licorice with marzipan, and we were snacking on them on our way to the Blue Lagoon while listening to Björk's jazz album, Gling-Gló. (A very fun part of being in Iceland is passing by every stranger and asking yourself, Is that Björk? Is that Björk? Please be Björk.) Then we got there and went straight into this opaque, milky-blue water; it was kind of like being in a luxurious version of that cloudy bath in Minority Report that [Samantha Morton] lies in. There was a mask bar in the lagoon, where you can apply a silica mud mask, an algae mask, or a mineral mask to your face, and it all felt very thick, goopy, and smooth on the skin. We're Asian and all have eczema, so we experienced a lot of relief afterward. It was very cute seeing families with members of all ages, including my children, wading around the lagoon together with spa masks on their face. Then Sheng—and this is very Sheng—started harvesting the silica off the walls and putting it on his face. Since it was free, we all copied him. I'm not sure if that was good for us or not.”

#6187. Airline Captain Defends 20-Year-Old Female Copilot After Fatal Learjet Crash

121pilot, our resident commercial airline pilot on Live And Let’s Fly, examines what we know about the crash of Learjet 60 N722BD and pushes back against the rush to blame its young first officer, Nathalia Filgueiras.

The crash of N722BD, a Learjet 60 operating on a charter flight, has drawn enormous attention. Much of that is understandable. We have extremely dramatic video of the aircraft descending almost vertically at a very high rate of speed, along with equally dramatic ATC audio recordings.

As is typical of the aviation YouTube community, many of whom I respect, people have been rushing to get videos out about this accident. What I really don’t care for, however, are the clickbait titles. Titles like “Could Any Pilot Have Saved This Learjet 60?” or “Lear 60 Florida Crash: It Happened Before” or “Expert Pilot Explains What Likely Caused SHOCKING Plane Crash in Florida” by Megyn Kelly.

These kinds of titles make me angry because, regardless of the actual content of the videos, they are misleading. The simple fact is that we know very little about this accident at this point, and certainly not enough to be speculating about a probable cause.

The aircraft, a Learjet Model 60 with nine people aboard, reported moderate turbulence and icing at Flight Level 350 and requested a climb to Flight Level 370. Moments later, the aircraft departed controlled flight, eventually entering a descent at an extraordinarily high rate of speed.

We know that the NTSB has recovered components of the horizontal stabilizer that separated from the aircraft, and widely circulated video appears to show the aircraft without this crucial component.

What we DON’T know is whether the aircraft flew into a thunderstorm. The weather imagery I’ve seen to date comes from sources that have time lags built into them and don’t necessarily represent the real-time weather picture. We don’t know what caused the horizontal stabilizer to separate, or even when that happened. Did it separate during the dive, or was its failure what initiated the dive? That’s an important distinction, and right now it’s an unknown.

We know the Learjet 60’s wing is sensitive to ice accumulation and that the aircraft is susceptible to a phenomenon called Mach tuck. We don’t know whether either played any role in this accident, or even whether the aircraft’s critical surfaces had accumulated ice.

We know the aircraft had been operating at higher altitudes, with a reported descent from Flight Level 410 to 350 before the final sequence of events. But without knowing the aircraft’s speed, configuration, weight, and other performance parameters, we cannot draw meaningful conclusions about its operating margins.

We know the captain was 55 years old and very experienced. We know the first officer was 20 years old and relatively inexperienced, but fully qualified to act as a second in command.

We know the CVR, or cockpit voice recorder, has been recovered, but we don’t yet know whether its contents can be successfully recovered or what information it might provide. We also know the aircraft was not equipped with a flight data recorder, or FDR. That means information about the aircraft’s speed, heading, pitch, roll, system status, and other parameters may remain unknown or will have to be reconstructed using external data sources and whatever information can be gleaned from the CVR.

But perhaps the most disturbing part of this entire event, aside from the tragic loss of life, has been the reaction of so many people who couldn’t explain the difference between a slat and a flap, yet have felt perfectly qualified to judge the performance of the first officer based on her age and gender.

In the Megyn Kelly video, she questions whether someone who isn’t even old enough to drink should have been acting as a pilot.

I think the better question is why we allow 18-year-olds to join the military and go into combat, but apparently don’t think they’re old enough to have a beer. Why can a 20-year-old warrant officer fly a Black Hawk full of troops into the maelstrom of a hot landing zone, but we think he or she can’t be trusted with alcohol?

Even more disgusting have been some of the reactions to the ATC recordings.

First, let me suggest that if you haven’t already listened to them, don’t. Second, and most importantly, as a 56-year-old male airline captain, I hear absolutely nothing in that recording, either in her voice or in her actions, that merits criticism.

I don’t think people who haven’t experienced it can appreciate just how incredibly violent and terrifying that initial descent must have been. In one recording, we go from a seemingly calm situation, with the crew requesting a climb, to a loss of control and a reported descent of approximately 8,000 feet per minute in about 10 seconds. Just 16 seconds later, the aircraft is in an overspeed condition, and the first officer reports a descent rate of 20,000 feet per minute. That’s an absolutely eye-watering number. It defies belief and would be utterly terrifying to any pilot. About 10 seconds later, she reports that they are going to crash into the ground. Not long after that, someone can be heard in the background reciting the Lord’s Prayer.

I don’t know this for certain, of course, but my suspicion is that somewhere during this sequence the crew became aware that the horizontal stabilizer had separated and that they had lost the ability to recover the aircraft.

If there is anything to be said about her performance as a pilot, it’s that she was clearly doing her job right up to the end.

We teach Aviate, Navigate, Communicate. Aviate means flying the airplane. Navigate means determining where you need to go and how to get there. Communicate means keeping the appropriate people informed.

In this situation, the captain was presumably concentrating on flying the aircraft while the first officer was communicating with ATC. That is exactly what we expect from a two-person crew in an emergency, assuming those were their respective roles at the time.

What’s more, in the absence of an FDR, the information she provided to ATC may prove absolutely crucial to understanding what happened. We may eventually discover that her actions and communications were instrumental in allowing the NTSB to piece together this accident. That information could well save lives in the future.

I also find it interesting, and troubling, that contrary to the media’s usual fixation on the captain, as though he’s flying the airplane solo, the exact opposite has happened here. The first officer has become the focus of an extraordinary amount of attention, even though we have not established who was flying the aircraft.

It’s been my absolute privilege to fly with a number of female pilots throughout my career, and not one of them has ever done anything less than a sterling job. Frankly, the airplane doesn’t care about your gender or the color of your skin. And when it comes to aviation, that’s exactly how it should be. We should care about qualifications and competence. That’s it.

If I step onto my jet tomorrow and find a young female first officer waiting for me, I’ll be just as happy to have her there as I would a young male. At this point in my career, flying with a young and relatively inexperienced first officer gives me the opportunity to act as a mentor and pass along some hard-won flying wisdom. That’s something I genuinely enjoy. Nathalia had earned her place in that cockpit. Not one iota of the solid evidence we have right now leads me to believe that this accident can or should be blamed on her.

It may well turn out that crew errors figure prominently in the probable cause. We simply don’t know yet. But if that turns out to be the case, it’s important to remember that the captain was the pilot in command. He was responsible for the operation of that aircraft, and the first officer was serving under his command. If poor decision-making put the aircraft into a situation from which there was no escape, the captain would bear the primary responsibility for those decisions.

But that’s a hypothetical. And right now, we don’t know that any such decisions were made.

We owe the nine people who lost their lives, their families, and the people who will eventually investigate this accident something better than speculation, sensationalism, and a rush to judgment.

121pilot is a pilot for a major U.S. commercial airline who offers analysis on industry news as well as occasional reflections on his own travels.

Yeah, no. There was no excuse for these pilots to thread the needle between two storm systems and risk safety in the process. Both overestimated the capabilities of their aircraft, one known to be prone to the issues experienced and proved fatal.

From a legal standpoint, the author is correct. We don’t know. However we have a reasonable scenario that is worth trying to prevent in the future….. icing conditions caused a dive which shredded the horizontal stabilizer in the back if the plane sending it into an unrecoverable dive.

Nope. A 20 year old should NEVER be the first officer. When DEI virtue signaling replaces common sense, bad things happen. Case in point. This is an absolute tragedy for all parties involved, but I never ever ever want a 20 year old at the controls (male or female). And to all the usual suspects (commenters like 1990, etc), I don’t want to hear the nonsense about age and military comparisons. The training of Air Force / Naval aviators is exponentially deeper than what we are talking about here. It’s like saying ‘I can drive a Toyota Corolla around the corner” to an F1 driver.

The issue here is not that she was female. The issue is that it was a very young co-pilot who showed signs of immaturity and questionable professional standards, not exactly surprising considering she was 20 years old. The comparison to Army helicopter pilots has some validity but less than you think. The Army is a very disciplined environment and certain things would simply not be tolerated that might be at a small charter operation. This is a chronic problem at the small, low paid charter companies. They have trouble retaining people who leave as soon as they can move up the ladder. So they have to replace them with whoever they can get. There is a term for the replacements, “seat fillers,” meaning people who lack the background and experience to do the job at a high level.

This is not an issue at places like NetJets, which is the largest charter operator and a career job. Good pay, benefits, schedules and a top notch training department. They get more than enough applications from very experienced pilots. They don’t have 20 year olds coming from Cessna 150s flying their aircraft.

This co-pilot was texting with her boyfriend ten minutes before the accident. They weren’t in clear air. They were dodging thunderstorms and dealing with ice. If there is ever a time for a pilot to be 100% focused on the task at hand, that is it.

This was not her first rodeo with ATC. The situation in the video linked at the bottom occurred a few months ago in New York. The basic knowledge about turbulence and how to report it to ATC is lacking. Chop and turbulence have different meanings. Moderate and severe turbulence have specific definitions and she did not understand it. Her response to the exasperated controller, “We were about to call you” is more like the language of a teenager than a professional pilot.

We will likely never know definitively why this accident happened. The aircraft was picking up ice but that should have been manageable with the deicing system. Was it turned on and if so, was it turned on early enough? They entered a climb but was it done too abruptly, causing them to stall the plane? Was it something else we don’t know?

They definitely entered a thunderstorm and would have had it painting on their radar for some time. Time lag is a non-issue here. But was the radar used correctly? The Lear 60 doesn’t have multi-scan radar as standard equipment and I doubt it was installed later. This means that the tilt control had to be operated manually. Manual tilt works very well but it takes some knowledge and experience to use properly.

Regardless of the cause, the ultimate responsibilty for everything that happens rests with the Captain. But crew experience, training and proficiency are always part of the puzzle that the investigation will look at.

I once was flying down to Cozumel on a beautiful, clear January morning. Smooth air and nothing but a few high puffy clouds. We were about 200 miles from the island and already saw on the radar that Cozumel had nothing painting in the area. The regional pilot (a male, btw) told the startled Mexican controller that they would have to hold because there was a thunderstorm over the airport. The controller asked incredulously about there being a thunderstorm there and the crew responded affirmitively. There was a pause and the controller came back and said Cozumel Tower says there is no storm at the airport. The regional crew eventually accepted this and continued. We had a good chuckle and figured the likely cause was that the regional had the radar selected to manual mode with the tilt too low, so they were painting a return of the island itself and thinking it was a thunderstorm. Sh*t happens out there, even to old pilots, and we all learn from our mistakes, 🙂

https://x.com/inversewire/status/2117340400021295110?a=MsD1TNoBXeVqCA5pHhQ&s=20

Thank you for your perspective, 121Pilot. It seemed like first officer, Nathalia Filgueiras, was a professional to the last moment. RIP to her and the others. Ideally, we can learn from the investigation and avoid such horrors from ever happening again.

#6186. Global Airlines Is “Fyre Festival”, Not Virgin Atlantic

Yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for New York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

The whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic launched in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

The fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

Let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that says pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following…

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter company which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have…

Travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

The truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most new people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

Everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

Getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

On real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

Their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

The app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

All the great, big airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

Tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

And in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

If Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

Let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and company books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so big time!

The business purports to be a home swap company, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his company ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

My only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

So yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or new seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a new golden age, again.

Gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott

His intrusion and snide comment ab0ut Simon Calder was entirely unnecessary. I have little respect for Asquith as it is, he doesn’t seem to actually “do” anything other than post Insta’s of slamming Champagne, and buying an Instagram account for the new venture is downright deceptive. Prove me wrong, I’m all for new carriers, but part of me wants it to fail just because of the insufferable “CEO”.

‘Global Airlines’ reminds me of the line from ‘The Producers’: “Under the right circumstances, a [person] could make more money with a flop than he could with a hit.”

This is why many say “hire for personality and train for skill.” James Asquith has failed this test with his attitude and stands little chance of building a culture within his company that can grow to compete with the likes of Virgin. I was always concerned that this airline was launching without any unique selling points at all. Now to read that what little was brought in from China Southern does not even work: it’s for me very sad to read. Substantial funding was needed to get this far and there seems to have been very little planning around the customer experience. I raised 350k externally to launch my last business, and that was not easy for me to do. So to imagine the capital sums that will be wasted here for all the unforced errors made, it’s so disheartening given it was foreseeable! There are so many case studies, even from Virgin with Virgin Nigeria and Virgin America to review! James Asquith seems to be very lazy and entitled. A great opportunity not afforded to many better qualified people (not me), has been thrown away!

While I agree with everything in this article, I also feel like immediately criticizing new entrants and disrupters is not fair. There is not a single person in aviation that wants to see less A380’s, that want les competition transatlantic, or fewer carriers. I appreciate Global, I appreciate BOOM, and I think it is just as sensational to criticize Global as it is for them to put on a metaphorical Fyre Fest in the sky. This is responsible reporting, but let’s also at some recognize the feat that getting this particular plane in the sky, with people, to NY was. Aviation was built on the backs of visionaries and risk-takers, I hope we will continue to celebrate that spirit.

I’m genuinely surprised that yours seems to the the only objectively credible take on this fiasco. I’ve watched a couple of the first flight review videos and the aircraft and service are laughable, yet the internet is still awash with “great to see!” and “Go Global!”, all blindly ignoring the current capabilities of the competition summarised above as if they don’t matter.

At least it’s given us a good laugh over the last few years but someone is losing money (hard to call anything sunk into this shambles an “investment”) and I imagine the flag carriers will be delighted as it makes them look stellar by comparison. Got to seriously question the judgement of anyone that wanted to get involved with Global. It’s all been smoke and mirrors from day one.

#6185. Some records in Ilhan Omar case will be released, judge says

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

A judge said he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

Judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

“This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg said.

The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

Boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he said next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”

The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

“You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg said.

Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump said last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

Separately, Boasberg said he may issue rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

For years Trump has said he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

#6183. Sweet: Deaf 5-Year-Old Bonds With American Airlines Flight Attendant And Gets A Surprise Welcome From CEO

A flight attendant signing with a young passenger is a lovely moment on its own. But seeing five-year-old Luca meet American Airlines CEO Robert Isom, who learned a few signs to greet him, made me smile even more. We spend plenty of time examining what airlines get wrong. Here is something American got right.

Luca is five years old, Deaf, and loves airplanes. In a video shared by American Airlines, a flight attendant communicates with him in sign language near the aircraft door and. again onboard. Watching Luca respond is delightful.

There is something particularly sweet about seeing a child discover that someone outside his family can communicate with him in his own language. The flight attendant takes the time to engage with Luca directly, and his reaction is precious.

The family later shared footage of a visit to American Airlines in Dallas, including a meeting with Isom.

According to his mother, Isom took the time to learn how to spell his name and sign “nice to meet you” in American Sign Language. He also gave Luca American Airlines trading cards, which she said he was very excited about.

Her explanation of why the meeting mattered was simple:

“I can’t tell you how much it means when someone takes that extra step to communicate with him.”

A post shared by CALLIE FOSTER (@thelacouple)

In another post about the visit, she described hundreds of American employees gathering to welcome Luca, with many having learned some sign language for him. She said the family had not known what American had planned and was overwhelmed by the reception.

That is quite a day for a little boy who loves airplanes.

These small gestures make a huge difference…isn’t that true of so many things in life?

Isom could have posed for a photograph, handed over the trading cards, and still called it a successful visit. Instead, he learned enough to introduce himself and greet Luca directly. Taking a little time beforehand allowed him to participate in the conversation rather than leave all the communicating to Luca’s parents.

The same goes for the employees who learned signs before welcoming him. It is easy to talk about the need to “care for people on life’s journey” (the current AA slogan). Here, they did something practical to make that happen.

As a father, I understand why his mother was so touched. When someone makes an effort for your child, you remember it. A brief interaction that an employee might regard as a small part of the workday can become something a family talks about long afterward.

And yes, American shared the encounter on social media. I am glad it did. There is room to recognize good hospitality even when an airline benefits from showing it.

Between the flight attendant signing with Luca and the welcome he received at American’s campus, this family has some wonderful memories to take home. I appreciated watching Isom make the effort too. Learning a greeting is a modest undertaking, but his mother’s account explains how much it meant. Well done to everyone at American who helped make Luca feel so welcome. This was a refreshing bit of airline news to watch.

#6182. Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

This week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a new strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the new strategic partnership for India was announced with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

That’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most important aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a new manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are big business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

In a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local company, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the new alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following…

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

To me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

The food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

In short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

#6180. American Airlines Offers “His” Free First Class Upgrade For $91, Then Tells Frequent Flyer To Delete His Complaint

An American Airlines frequent flyer complained about a $91 first class upgrade offer and received a response asking him to delete his post. That might sound like an airline trying to suppress criticism, but there is a much more sensible explanation: his screenshot exposed his reservation details. As for the inexpensive upgrade itself, I see a pragmatic opportunity rather than a scandal.

This hit my algorithm on X (and apparently VFTW too), but an AAdvantage Executive Platinum member took to the platform to express frustration that American was offering paid first class upgrades for $91 while his complimentary upgrade had not cleared (this was on a short 551-mile flight from Dallas to El Paso).

American acknowledged his frustration, then added:

“Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.”

The response attracted attention, but the screenshot included the passenger’s reservation confirmation number. That is a good reason to remove it and not a sign of AA trying to hide from its transactional upgrade policy!

We can understand why this feels frustrating. Your loyalty is genuinely appreciated, and we're sorry this experience left you feeling overlooked. Please delete this from public view and join us in DM.

— americanair (@AmericanAir) November 18, 2026

It seems obvious to me that American was trying to protect the passenger here.

A reservation confirmation number, often called a record locator or PNR, is something you should keep private. Combined with your last name, it can potentially allow someone to retrieve your booking. Depending on the airline and its security controls, that could expose information about your trip or allow someone to interfere with it. At least with AA you also need your birthdate in order to access the record online or on the AA app.

Posting a screenshot to make a point about upgrades should not mean giving strangers an opportunity to tamper with your reservation…and some losers have far too much on their hand (which I’ve found out the hard way and why even when I “live blog” I never truly live blog).

American could have explained this much better. A simple request to remove the screenshot because it contained private booking information would have avoided the ambiguity. The passenger could then have reposted his complaint with those details obscured.

As to the underlying complaint, I understand why an Executive Platinum member would be frustrated. If you have directed substantial business to an airline and are waiting for an upgrade, watching the airline offer that seat for a relatively small payment can feel like your loyalty counts for very little.

But I am not going to attack American for selling inexpensive upgrades. This is the business model now, and I use it to my advantage when I fly AA. If the economy fare is attractive and American subsequently offers a reasonably priced upgrade, I can evaluate the total cost and decide whether first class is worth it. Sometimes it is. Sometimes I am perfectly happy staying where I am, like on a recent flight where I ended up with an entire row to myself. Oddly, sometimes the cost of the upgrade is more than buying the ticket outright…I have no explanation for that.

That is a much more straightforward transaction than spending more throughout the year in the hope that an airline will eventually reward me with a seat it would still prefer to sell.

Fundamentally, a complimentary upgrade that has not cleared, even at the gate, is not a seat that already belongs to the elite member. We can debate all day long about how prominently or aggressively airlines market upgrades when frequent flyers are waiting when upgrades are dangled like a carrot on a stick, but passengers can respond to that change by reconsidering how much they are willing to spend pursuing status.

I am a free agent, and it is liberating. More people should try it. Two years in, I’m more happy than ever (and flying in first class more than ever on domestic flights). I  choose a flight because the schedule works or because the price makes sense, without worrying that I am depriving my preferred airline of another qualifying flight or dollar toward next year’s status.

If American offers a good fare and an inexpensive first class upgrade, great. I can take advantage of it. I do not need to be an Executive Platinum member to recognize a good deal (as much as I miss the oneworld emerald lounge access when traveling internationally).

That does not mean status has become worthless. I still receive occasional complimentary upgrades as both an American Airlines Gold and United Airlines Gold member. I appreciate those upgrades very much, especially when I am not expecting them. But I do not build my travel plans around them. Hoping for a free upgrade seems futile in many cases even with top-tier status, particularly when the airline business model now centers on actively trying to sell the remaining seats.

For me, an occasional upgrade is a pleasant bonus on a flight I was otherwise willing to fly in economy class on. But upgrades are not a compelling reason to keep spending more with one airline when another offers a better flight….sorry, but the value proposition is gone.

American Airlines could have been clearer about why it wanted this passenger to delete his post. Still, the exposed reservation details provide a sensible explanation, and I would not characterize the request as an attempt to silence criticism.

As for the $91 upgrade, I am pragmatically happy those offers exist. They give me another way to sit up front without organizing my travel around the pursuit of top-tier status. I still enjoy the occasional complimentary upgrade, but choosing flights on my own terms, and paying for a better seat when the price is right, has been far more satisfying than chasing an upgrade that may never clear. Try it, you’ll like it.

#6179. JetBlue Adds New Destination in Latin America, Caribbean Expansion

JetBlue is growing its presence in Central America and the Caribbean.

For the first time ever, the carrier will serve the Honduran capital of Tegucigalpa. Starting Feb. 25, 2027, flights from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, will arrive at Palmerola International Airport in Comayagua, which serves Tegucigalpa.

Currently, JetBlue’s only destination in Honduras is San Pedro Sula, in the country’s northwest.

On Feb. 23, the carrier will launch service between Fort Lauderdale and George Town, Grand Cayman, in the Cayman Islands.

Both routes will operate daily, using a mix of Airbus A320 and A220 aircraft.

JetBlue will also offer limited-time daily service from Fort Lauderdale to Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago, between Jan. 29 and Feb. 15. The connection will help travelers reach the islands during Carnival, the airline said.

“We’re grateful for the way customers across South Florida continue to embrace JetBlue, and we’re committed to delivering even more of the destinations and travel options they’re looking for,” Daniel Shurz, JetBlue’s senior vice president of revenue, network, and enterprise planning, said in a news release. “With new international service to Honduras and Grand Cayman, we’re strengthening Fort Lauderdale’s role as a key gateway to Latin America and the Caribbean, making it easier for customers to reconnect with loved ones, explore new places, and travel across our growing network.”

American has prioritized Latin America as demand from U.S. markets, especially Miami, grows. The carrier just recently launched service to Barranquilla and Cali in Colombia and will add Barcelona, Venezuela, to its network in January.

#6178. These incoming members of Congress have been here before

Rep.-elect Chris Rabb, D-Pa., greets current members of Congress in the Capitol on Nov. 11. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

When Rep.-elect Chris Rabb first worked on Capitol Hill in the 1990s, it didn’t exactly inspire him to want to go into politics.

“I said, ‘Oh, this is how the sausage is made? I should be a vegan,’” the Pennsylvania Democrat recalled.

Working for Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman elected as a U.S. senator, Rabb saw threats and “just vile things” directed at her.

“My entrée to service behind the scenes was seeing voluminous amounts of violence, hate speech and death threats against my boss, and I thought to myself, ‘Why would anyone want to serve?’” he said.

During his time in the state legislature starting in 2017, Rabb “fell in love with public service, despite the vitriol.” Now, the democratic socialist describes coming to Congress as “surreal,” as he succeeds retiring Rep. Dwight Evans in a deep-blue district based in West Philadelphia.

Rabb is one of more than a dozen incoming members who have worked on the Hill before, ranging from interns to chiefs of staff and everything in between.

Unlike some in the 100-plus-strong freshman class, they already know their way around the hallways. And Rabb has some advice for his new colleagues: “Treat your staff well. Take care of your staff; they’ll take care of you.”

Here are some of the former staffers who will join the House in January.

A couple years ago, Killin was working as chief of staff to former second gentleman Doug Emhoff. But she started out on the Hill.

“It is helpful to know, as I joke, where the bathrooms are, but I still feel like I have a lot to learn,” said the Army veteran, who unseated Republican Rep. Jeff Crank in a Colorado Springs-area district.

She served as the top staffer for three House Democrats: Donna Shalala of Florida, Carolyn Maloney of New York and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington.

“I’ve actually opened up two freshman offices, so it’s helpful to have done that before,” Killin said.

White will be just the third person in modern times to hold the job of nonvoting D.C. delegate. He replaces retiring Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton — also his former boss.

Before his time on the D.C. Council, he worked as her legislative counsel, watching her navigate a role with limited power in her perennial fight for statehood.

“I need to make sure I’m developing a national profile for this seat,” he said, vowing to continue the quest for full representation even as President Donald Trump seeks to exert more control over the District.

One of just a few Republican women in the freshman class, Gruters said she “never in a million years” imagined coming to Congress herself, despite her years as a staffer.

She will replace retiring Rep. Vern Buchanan in Florida’s 16th District, after once serving as his operations director. She also worked as district director for Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla.

“I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Gruters, whose husband leads the Republican National Committee.

Rogers added another title to his résumé last week: freshman class president.

His fellow incoming Republicans tapped him for the role. Not so long ago, he was working for the Senate Judiciary Committee, fresh off a stint at the white-shoe law firm White & Case.

In 2025 he served as general counsel for Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., and plans to keep pushing for a bill he helped draft that aims to crack down on foreign surrogacy contracts. “We are currently selling American children to China, our No. 1 adversary,” Rogers said, describing it as “deplorable.”

Rogers will succeed retiring GOP Rep. Neal Dunn in the Florida Panhandle.

García’s run for her boss’s seat drew controversy from the start. When Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García, D-Ill., waited to publicly announce his retirement until after the filing deadline in Illinois had already passed, critics blasted him for effectively boxing out other candidates and clearing the way for his chief of staff.

He faced a rare formal disapproval vote in the House over the move. But García has insisted she is more than a hand-picked successor, saying on her campaign website that she has “delivered solutions rooted in lived experience.”

The son of Ghanaian immigrants, Boafo is a state delegate who has lobbied on the Hill for tech company Oracle.

He also worked as campaign manager for Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, earning an endorsement from the retiring longtime Democrat and campaign cash from groups aligned with him.

Boafo prevailed in a crowded primary, even as Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi threw her weight behind a different candidate, former Capitol Police officer Harry Dunn.

Sell worked under then-House Agriculture Chair Larry Combest during the 2000 crop insurance overhaul and the fight over the 2002 farm bill. He later joined his former boss in launching an agricultural lobbying firm, Combest, Sell and Associates.

Once a precocious child magician who wrote his own book of tricks, Lasher also got an early start in politics.

“I feel supremely fortunate to have wandered into Jerry Nadler’s political orbit as a teenager 30 years ago, and then to have worked in his congressional office a decade later,” Lasher wrote in an opinion piece for City & State New York.

Backed by the retiring Nadler, the self-described “nerd” beat out a couple of big names in the primary, including a Kennedy family heir. Another former boss endorsed him, too: Gov. Kathy Hochul. Before serving as a New York state assemblyman, Lasher worked as her policy director.

Villegas ousted GOP Rep. David Valadao in a closely watched race in the San Joaquin Valley.

A decade ago, he was an intern for Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif. And the progressive also interned for former California state Rep. Rudy Salas, who made unsuccessful bids to unseat Valadao in 2022 and 2024.

A San Diego City councilmember, Von Wilpert flipped the seat held by Republican Rep. Darrell Issa, who decided not to run for reelection under a map redrawn by Democrats.

When she worked for the National Labor Relations Board in 2016, she was detailed to the House Education and Labor Committee, working under ranking member Robert C. Scott, D-Va.

Jackie Wang and Nick Eskow contributed to this report.

#6177. This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

In the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

But now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

As an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

#6176. Türkiye Just Announced a New Golden Visa Starting at $150,000

Türkiye is one of the world’s most visited countries, straddling the vibrant crossroads of Europe, Asia, and the Middle East. With sun-soaked Mediterranean beaches, Ottoman-influenced gastronomy, historic mosques, and bustling bazaars, it’s no surprise that the country attracted nearly 64 million visitors in 2025. But if your love of the country has you considering a prolonged vacation (or perhaps a second home), the government’s new golden visa might be a good fit—so long as you have $150,000 to spend.

On November 17, Türkiye's president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan signed a decision to enact a new foreign investor visa. The program offers two pathways: a $150,000 investment for a three-year residence permit, or $200,000 for a five-year stay (both of which can extend to the applicant’s spouse and dependents).

As for where your money goes, you can deposit your funds in a local bank, buy government debt instruments, contribute to a pension plan, or invest in real estate or venture capital funds. No matter which pathway you select, you must hold your investment for at least half the visa term (as in, 1.5 years for the three-year visa or 2.5 years for the five-year visa). That means you could potentially withdraw your investment as early as after 18 months, according to IMI Daily, an investment migration trade publication.

The president’s announcement doesn't detail when or how foreigners can begin to apply, or the specific documents required. However, applications for the country’s other residence-by-investment permits require documents such as proof of financial means and health insurance, according to the government’s Investment and Finance Office.

If you don’t want to shell out $150,000, Türkiye offers other (renewable) relocation pathways. You may qualify for a two-year Short-Term Residence Permit for reasons such as tourism and university-sponsored research. Or, if your spouse is Turkish, you could apply for the three-year Family Residence Permit. Once you’ve lived in the country continuously for eight years, you’ll be eligible to apply for the indefinite Long-Term Residence Permit, which grants you almost all the same perks as citizenship, minus civic duties such as the ability to vote and mandatory military service.

It's important to note that the new golden visa does not provide permanent citizenship. If you’re hoping to find your way into a passport, get ready to spend more. Türkiye’s citizenship-by-investment pipeline will require you to buy a home worth at least $400,000, invest at least $500,000 in sectors such as government bonds or venture capital funds, or, alternatively, help create at least 50 jobs.

Over the last few years, the influx of new residency-by-investment programs has made it easier for wealthy travelers to relocate internationally. In New Zealand, you can invest $1 million New Zealand Dollars (about $567,300) in exchange for a three-year work-to-residency track. For Mediterranean living, Greece offers a five-year permit for a 250,000 euro (about $291,120) investment in a startup. Or, for a more affordable option, Paraguay has a permanent residency program for those who can invest $150,000 in “tourism projects” or $200,000 in stocks or real estate—putting it in line with Türkiye as one of the more affordable relocation options.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6175. Review: Air France Business Class Lounge – Paris (CDG) – Terminal 2E, Hall L (Now Sans Sauna…)

You can read a more comprehensive review below, but here are some key points:

I’m big fan of this lounge..it’s a nice one even without the controversial sauna. Here are some photos:

> Read More: Air France Closes Paris Lounge Sauna After Passengers Apparently Turned It Into A Sex Den

Although I’ve been to this lounge several times over the years, my last formal review was when it first opened in 2019, which I’ve included as a point of reference below.

I’ve showcased stock photos of the lounge before, but the photos below are all my own. Because the spa in the La Premiere Lounge closed early, I was offered a spa treatment in this new business class lounge. Although it was in a different section of the terminal, I was driven over and did not have to re-clear security.

The lounge is located on the upper level just past the security checkpoint. As you enter the lounge, you’ll be greeted by a moving sign that resembles a glass of champagne.

Since the purpose of my visit to the lounge was to use the spa, let’s start there. Immediately upon arrival I was ushered into a treatment room and given a 15-minute facial. The lady who performed the facial was chatty and gave me a laundry list of cream recommendations, bluntly stating that my face was too dry. Normally, you can sign up for these treatments on a first-come, first-served basis when you reach the lounge. Advance reservations are not permitted.

This lounge is spread out over one (very) large area with couches and chairs scattered throughout the lounge. Perhaps my visit, on December 23rd, was not a typical Saturday evening, but the lounge was less than 1/4 full. The entire rear half of the lounge was virtually empty.

The lounge manager saw I was taking pictures and knew I was a La Premiere passenger, so he beckoned me to follow him into a room marked “Private”. The room, he explained, was reserved for top-tier elites (by request) or special VIP guests.

In the center of the lounge is a beautiful dining room called Le Balcon with velvet couches and brass accents. It serves as a place to eat and a cocktail bar in the evening.

Buffets are stationed throughout the lounge with a selection of beverages and hot and cold food items.

At the far end of the lounge is an open kitchen in which a special dish of the day is prepared.

With the exception of the cocktail bar, alcohol is self-serve and champagne (Laurent Perrier) is available.

Even more than a facial, I would have loved to use the sauna in this lounge. Sadly, a guest had become ill the day before and vomited in it. Thus, it was quarantined pending sterilization. So much for that idea….

> Read More: A New Airport Lounge With A Sauna

Shower suites and restrooms were also available.

(This is a handicapped shower…they do not all look like this).

Next to the Clarins Spa was a rest area with chairs designed for napping. Don’t forget to set your alarm if you use one of these!

In all honesty, I liked this lounge a lot but liked the decor of the Terminal 2E, Hall M lounge better. The dining area / cocktail bar in the center of this lounge is beautiful. Everything else is just nice. Air France offers excellent lounges in Paris that are worth stopping in at before your flight whether you are flying in business class or simply have SkyTeam elite status. Don’t forget to sign up for a complimentary facial or massage…it is worthwhile.

#6174. Wander.com: Best Luxury Take On Airbnb (With Real Value Too?)

At first, the big hotel chains of the world laughed off Airbnb and vacation rentals. No seriously, they did. Now, they all compete in the vacation rental business and act like it was always the plan.

The problem for the traveler, is that almost all of the newer entrants just plug into a massive pipeline of already existing vacation homes and apartments and pop them on their own branded website with no added luxury, differentiation, amenity or expertise in curation.

There’s no huge unlock of new places or highly curated places that you could virtually always stamp as worth recommending to a friend, the way you’d rate an Aman, St. Regis, or Four Seasons hotel.

This is precisely where Wander.com comes in, and it’s by far my favorite luxe vacation rental platform to date. The fact that it’s boutique and limited is what makes it, at least for me. And, the $350 off Wander promo code doesn’t hurt either.

Wander is a vacation rental company which truly hand picks every property that it lists, and has the exclusive listing on. Crucially, each of the vacation properties undergoes a sort of ‘Wander’ transformation to conform with brand standards for wifi, amenity, style and vibe.

It’s above my pay-grade as a blogger on this topic, but it seems like Wander co-invests in the real estate portfolio’s, or partners with owners in a unique way that’s far more integrated than others.

Where are they? Most Wander.com properties are scattered across the US, from the shores of Malibu to the great National Parks in Wyoming and all along the Eastern seaboard too. Hawaii is also a recent addition. New destinations keep popping up!

Each of their properties feels uniquely wonderful and aspirational, and I’d say all have a very modern and contemporary slant to luxury. Grandma’s cabinets are not in any of these homes, but Tesla chargers are. One nice touch: each Wander offers a dedicated workspace with desk, chair, monitors and lightning fast wifi.

I completely respect that all tastes are individual, but the interiors and setups of these homes much more reflect my personal tastes, more minimalist chic, than many less curated vacation rental options.

Most Wander properties are around $1000 a night. Some will be half that, some will be double. On its face, that’s intimidating to many, but when you factor in the number of bedrooms and features it’s really reasonable. Families, or multi-family get togethers… amazing.

All Wander.com properties are at least two bedrooms and many are four, five or even twelve. One is an entire island with multiple residential complexes. For me, I love these sort of getaways for catching up with family or friends, and I never mind when other people are contributing too.

We’ve had some of our best ever vacations renting a house in Palm Springs for weeks or months at a time. Often, family or friends want in too, so we split the house and end up with two bedrooms each for under $500 per night.

We’ve used these bonus rooms and features to socialize or catch up with people in the serenity of the home, not annoyed by service, crowded pools or tight room setups. For a longer stay, I absolutely hate having to rely on a hotel kitchen for every meal. I love to hit a local market and grill with family or guests.

Wander is offering $350 off first bookings, which is a great way to get started. To browse the homes, you simply download the Wander app and start doom scrolling. When you find one you’re ready to book, the process is very self explanatory and easy to share with others.

I’m personally a fan of virtually California vacation and the properties offered on the platform cover everything from Palm Springs to Napa and all in between in stunning form. The $350 off is a solid discount and combined with new property discounts, which are frequent, there is a lot to love. You can browse Wander and download the app here.

If you don’t see the Wander.com discount in your account, you can add promo code AKFVDFD7 once the app is downloaded.

#6173. Dozens of Early Black Friday Deals Have Landed—Save Up to 60% on Travel Essentials

Good news, travelers—dozens of early Black Friday deals are already here. This means you can save on editor-recommended luggage, clothing and shoes, tech essentials, home goods, and just about everything else before your next trip (and before the holidays even begin). Cyber Week officially kicks off on Black Friday, November 27, but tons of early deals from brands we love like Away, Cozy Earth, and Nordstrom are already live—with some discounts as high as 50% off right now.
