We get it — mastering points and miles is no easy feat. You may have seen our guide to getting started with points and miles, but what happens once you're ready to cash those points in for a trip?

Maximizing points and miles to travel luxuriously without breaking the bank doesn’t need to be laborious and time-consuming. In fact, there are various tools available that make it easier to find hotel and flight award availability.

With these tools, you can use your points to travel where you want, when you want and how you want in 2027 (and beyond) without spending hours searching for availability.

Here are 14 of the best apps and websites that make award travel redemptions easier and less stressful.

What it does: Finds flight award availability based on your itinerary.

What it costs: The basic plan is free, but you really unlock the best features with a paid membership. Right now, TPG has a special offer: Roame.travel is offering TPG readers 40% off the Friends of Roame Pro membership with code "THEPOINTSGUY," which brings the regular price down to $94 per year (from $156).

When you sign up for a free Roame account, you can search more than 25 airline programs for instant, real-time award availability.

After clicking a flight option, you can see the points required to book, as well as the available transfer partners and recommended credit cards to help you earn the points you need. You can even add your existing credit cards to your virtual wallet to get recommendations.

With a paid membership, you can also track points pricing with route alerts.

As always, we recommend confirming award availability before transferring points.

Related: The complete guide to searching award space on Roame.travel

What it does: Helps travelers find airline award space.

What it costs: There is a free version that alerts you to seat availability on a specific flight, but you can get additional alerts and better search functions with the Basic ($6.99 per month), Premium ($12.99 per month) or Elite ($19.99 per month) membership options. There are discounts if you choose to pay annually.

And there's an ExpertFlyer discount exclusively for TPG readers: New users can get 30% off any annual subscription.

ExpertFlyer (owned by TPG's parent company, Red Ventures) is a helpful tool for viewing airline schedules, seat maps and flight statuses across more than 400 airlines, as well as award and upgrade availability on select carriers. You can set seat alerts to help snag your preferred seat if it isn't available when you book your flight.

Related: How to use ExpertFlyer alerts to snag a better seat

A free account lets you set one alert at a time, but you will need a Basic, Premium or Elite membership to run an award search. Once you are logged in with a paid account, you can search using the "Awards & Upgrades" tab. When you enter your travel details and select the airline you'd like to fly, you'll see the fare classes that ExpertFlyer can search alongside a description.

When you click the search button at the bottom of the screen, ExpertFlyer presents you with a list of the available flights broken down by date. Once you have the date, flight number and fare class, you can book your flight online or by calling the airline directly. If the flight you're looking to book doesn't have seats available in your preferred fare class, you can set an alert, and ExpertFlyer will email you if a seat is released, taking the legwork out of award searches.

ExpertFlyer's expanded Systemwide Upgrades feature lets American Airlines elite members with systemwide upgrades search availability up to 330 days out across multiple regions. This feature is only available with ExpertFlyer's Elite plan. Basic and Premium members can still search systemwide upgrade space one route at a time through the “Awards & Upgrades” tab.

What it does: Tracks hotel award availability at Hyatt, Hilton, IHG and Marriott properties.

What it costs: Free for basic membership; $3.99 per month for a Gold membership and $7.99 per month for a Platinum membership (though there's a 40% off Thanksgiving promotion if you elect to pay annually).

MaxMyPoint is a website that lets you check award availability for Hyatt, Hilton, IHG and Marriott properties worldwide. It takes the guesswork out of award redemption searches by showing real-time award pricing and availability.

The homepage shows popular properties, but you can filter by hotel brand, location, price and more to narrow down your results. You can also search date-based deals or use the map search feature to search multiple hotels in a single destination.

Once you choose a property, you can view a calendar that displays available points pricing and the lowest cash rate. This allows you to plan your trip around the dates with the best points pricing.

After you select your check-in date, you’ll automatically be redirected to the property’s website to start the booking process. If you can’t find the availability you are looking for, you can register for a free account and set up an alert to receive an email if availability changes.

Paid memberships come with additional features, including more frequent and more detailed alerts.

What it does: Displays award pricing in Google Flights.

What it costs: Free for a standard plan, $9.99 per month or $99.99 per year for a Pro plan. If you want to pay annually, there's also a paid option for alerts only, which costs $34.99 per year.

Points Path is a browser extension that displays award pricing alongside cash prices for select airlines in Google Flights. The free version includes points versus cash pricing for Alaska Airlines, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, JetBlue and United Airlines.

It also tells you which transferable points can be used with the airlines it supports, as well as when to book at a paid rate or with points. Once you select an itinerary, you can book it directly with the airline using points or cash, as you would with Google Flights.

Related: How to use the Points Path extension to compare cash and award rates in Google Flights

Points Path simplifies the decision of when to use cash or miles to buy airline tickets. Points Path Pro unlocks additional features such as price alerts, access to additional airline programs and customizable points valuations.

The browser extension is compatible with Chrome, Safari, Microsoft Edge, Opera, Brave and Arc.

What it does: Finds flight award availability based on your itinerary.

What it costs: There is a free version, but for real-time availability, you can purchase a Standard ($10.75 per month) or Premium ($21.67 per month) membership. These discounts are available when you pay annually. Concierge services are available starting at $200 per passenger.

TPG readers get seven months free on Standard Annual membership with code "THEPOINTSGUY7."

Point.me's robust interface searches for award flights across more than 30 loyalty programs and more than 150 airlines.

By entering your itinerary details, Point.me will display award availability, including which transfer partner offers the most value for your buck.

In addition to the free and paid versions, you can book one-on-one sessions with one of Point.me's expert consultants who can assist you with flight bookings, points strategies, elite status and mileage runs and more.

American Express cardholders can access a limited version of Point.me for free. As with the full version, you can search for award flight availability, but you will only see results from Amex transfer partners. This is a good way to try Point.me for free if you have Membership Rewards points that you want to transfer to an airline loyalty program to purchase tickets.

What it does: Helps you maximize your points by finding the best flight redemptions.

What it costs: Free for the basic plan; $99 per year for the premium plan (but there's a current promotion for $20 off).

Pointhound takes the guesswork (and hours of searching) out of turning your points and miles into award flights. The site’s search tool helps you find the best deals by displaying preferred booking options for a designated route and date.

For example, if you search for a flight from John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG), Pointhound will display your flight results alongside all available booking options.

If you know you want to fly Air France but don’t have enough Flying Blue miles, you can see which programs transfer to Air France partners, including those that have current transfer bonuses.

Once you’ve chosen a route and booking option, Pointhound will walk you through the points transfer and booking process. (You still book directly through the airline; Pointhound gives you the instructions on how to do it.)

If you want to stay informed about the latest flight deals, you can sign up to receive flight alerts from specific airports via email.

What it does: Searches for real-time award flight and hotel availability.

What it costs: Free for unlimited basic searches, $19.99 per month or $119.95 per year for Premium (though there are Black Friday promotions).

PointsYeah streamlines hotel and airline award bookings by searching all major credit cards, award programs and booking portals in under 20 seconds. You can view results from more than 20 airline programs and six major hotel programs.

Once you've chosen a flight, PointsYeah will display all available booking options. If you already have enough points, you can book directly with the airline; however, PointsYeah will show the amount of points you'd need to transfer from various credit card programs, including details on current transfer bonuses.

You can create flight and hotel alerts. Basic accounts get up to four flight and hotel price alerts, as well as five multi-region alerts for a 30-day search window.

Premium members get up to 32 flight alerts, 30 hotel alerts and up to 150 multi-region alerts for a 90-day search window. When you upgrade to Premium, you also get access to United Airlines upgrade alerts, expanded date and destination availability when you search and the ability to set custom values for your points currencies.

What it does: Provides real-time search results across multiple airports and travel dates simultaneously.

What it costs: Free for the basic plan; $12.99 per month or $109.99 per year for AwardTool Pro (with Black Friday discounts available).

If your travel dates and destinations are flexible, AwardTool can display results for multiple flights in a single search. If you're extra flexible, you can utilize the Panorama feature to view award pricing by region rather than a specific destination or the Deals feature to see the best award rates from your chosen airport to anywhere in the world.

When you upgrade to AwardTool Pro, you unlock access to additional and expanded search capabilities, up to 100 award alerts, unlimited Panorama alerts and live seat map availability.

What it does: Gondola helps you find the best hotel deals and use your points to book.

Gondola is a free AI-powered hotel booking tool that tracks your points and miles balances to help you maximize your rewards. When you search for your travel dates and destination, the results will display cash and points pricing, along with ratings to help you determine which is the better value.

You'll see results from major hotel groups like Marriott, Hilton, Hyatt, IHG, Accor and more.

Once you've chosen a property, Gondola will direct you to the hotel's website to book award stays directly with the hotel. For paid reservations, Gondola will book the hotel on your behalf, allowing you to earn the usual points and elite benefits, along with between 3% and 7% cash back in the form of Gondola Cashback for every stay.

Gondola will also monitor your bookings and alert you if the price drops, so you can rebook at the lower price.

What it does: Checks flight award availability based on your itinerary and preferred airline.

What it costs: Free for five economy award availability searches per day; $3.39 per month for a Premium subscription or $9.99 per month for a First Class subscription, with discounts for annual payments.

SeatSpy is an easy-to-use website that checks award availability across 10 airlines, most of which are not U.S.-based carriers.

Select your airline, departure and end destination airports, then hit “Search” to see availability across the next 12 months.

SeatSpy is free to use if you’re only searching for economy availability. Where the product really shines, however, is in its premium subscriptions.

The entry-level subscription, Premium, allows unlimited searches across all fares and up to four active alerts sent via email, WhatsApp and Telegram. It also includes AwardWallet integration, so you can track how many points you have to redeem.

First Class includes everything in the Premium plan, plus unlimited alerts sent instantly instead of hourly, along with SMS alerts and "experience alerts."

Both subscriptions offer a “Where Can I Go” search feature that shows all destinations with award availability from your departure airport on the travel dates you select.

It may have few features when compared to other services on this list, but in terms of simplicity, it’s a great site — especially if you’re looking at Europe-based airlines.

What it does: Displays award seat availability on domestic and international flights across fare classes.

What it costs: Free for the basic version and $12.99 monthly for the Pro version, which includes Rooms.aero access for hotel award searches.

Seats.aero regularly refreshes award space across dozens of airline programs and provides results for the next month or two.

The Pro version allows you to search up to a year in advance, set up unlimited alerts (whereas free users get only five) and receive SMS notifications when award availability turns up.

Related: How I use Seats.aero every day to find the best airline award availability in seconds

What it does: Displays hotel award availability across several major hotel brands.

What it costs: Free for the basic version; if you want the paid Pro version, you can get it through your Seats.aero membership.

Rooms.aero works similarly to its counterpart, Seats.aero. Users can search seven major hotel programs — Choice Privileges, Hilton Honors, World of Hyatt, IHG One Rewards, Marriott Bonvoy, I Prefer Hotel Rewards and Wyndham Rewards — for hotel award availability across certain dates or destinations.

Related: How to use Rooms.aero to find the best hotel award availability

Rooms.aero uses a valuation system to indicate whether you are getting good, average or poor value for your points for a given redemption. You can also filter by points program and the maximum number of points per night. When you choose a hotel, you'll see a calendar view with points and cash rates.

You can also use Rooms.aero to set availability alerts to notify you when a specific hotel or destination has points availability. With a Pro account, you get access to advanced search filters, SMS alerts and more.

What it does: Displays points, miles and cash pricing for flights and hotels.

What it costs: Free for a basic membership; $14.99 for a one-time “Trip Pass” valid for three days; and $12.50 per month (or $150 annually) for a premium membership.

Awayz helps you make the most of your hard-earned points and miles by showing when to redeem points and when to pay cash. You can use the Awayz search tool to find specific flight routes or hotels in specific destinations. Awayz will then display live award availability and cash rates so you can make a side-by-side comparison.

You can use the site’s robust filtering system to display certain hotel chains, transferable award programs and even those that qualify for free night certificates.

For flights, you can filter to see only certain airlines, choose the time of day you’d prefer to travel and even indicate which aircraft type you’d prefer. You can also update your “wallet” with the credit cards and reward balances you currently have, so it can tailor your results further.

Related: How to use Awayz to improve your hotel award searches

A free membership includes five hotel and five airline searches per month. An Awayz Trip Pass (great for one-time planning) includes 50 hotel searches, 50 flight searches and 10 award availability alerts for a one-time fee of $14.99. An Awayz Premium membership includes 500 hotel searches, 100 flight searches and 30 award availability alerts, among other perks.

What it does: Finds flight schedules and prices, with several filtering options, for most major airlines.

Google Flights is your one-stop shop for finding the best flight for your schedule and budget.

You can search flight schedules and pricing across most major airlines and sort results based on price, duration, number of stops, fare class and airlines, among other options. You can also set flight price alerts.

One of the best tools within Google Flights is Google Flights Explore.

Google Flights Explore lets you enter only your departure city, then use the interactive map to choose your destination based on current pricing.

Google Flights does not display points pricing (unless you use the Points Path plugin we mentioned earlier in this article), but that doesn’t mean it can’t help you find award space. You’ll still have to book directly through the airline, but you can save valuable search time by narrowing down your options through Google Flights first.

For example, if you have a bank of points and miles with a Star Alliance, Oneworld or SkyTeam partner airline, you can filter search results by alliance to see routing options. Or, you may find a nearby airport with better pricing that you wouldn’t have searched for otherwise.

The great thing about all these tools is that you can use them together to find award flights and free hotel nights.

No matter which combination of sites and apps you use, you’ll find that they take the guesswork out of award redemptions and put you on the fast track to becoming an expert in redeeming points and miles for your 2027 travels.

#6121. End Of An Era: American Retires Boeing 777 Flagship First Class

American Airlines has just officially “retired” its Flagship First product on the Boeing 777-300ER, meaning that no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore. The good news is that an updated business class product is in the process of being rolled out, and that’s something that should benefit a lot of travelers.

As I’ve covered in the past, American is in the process of eliminating its “premium” first class product, and that change was just implemented for flights as of this week on the carrier’s biggest planes.

Specifically, the Boeing 777-300ER is American’s “flagship” aircraft, with 20 of the planes in the fleet. As of this week, the airline is no longer selling first class on these planes. Now, plenty of 777-300ERs with these cabins are still flying around, as American has just started reconfiguring its 777-300ERs with new cabins, including the new business class.

Still, for flights effective immediately, first class seats are just being sold as standard business class seats, and any business class passenger can select seats in the first two rows (you’d think they’d try to charge extra or at least reserve them for select elite members, but nope). So there will no longer be a differentiated soft product… not that there was much of a difference as of late anyway!

I expect we’ll continue to see these planes flying around well into late 2027, or possibly even into 2028, depending on how fast the retrofit project happens. American’s dedicated first class ground product has also largely been discontinued, as Flagship First Dining has turned into Flagship Dining, so a la carte lounge dining is now available to eligible business class passengers as well.

It’s great that these planes will be getting new business class suites, as they’ll also be the aircraft belonging to a US carrier with the most business class seats, as they’ll have 70 of them… that’s lot!

While American has now eliminated its international first class product, it’s worth emphasizing that the airline still technically has a “premium” first class, in the sense of a cabin above business class.

Specifically, American still has its specially configured Airbus A321T aircraft, which are used primarily for flights between New York (JFK) and Los Angeles (LAX) and San Francisco (SFO). The planes have 10 reverse herringbone seats spread across five rows, in a 1-1 configuration.

American also plans to eliminate this product, as the A321Ts will be reconfigured into standard A321 domestic configuration aircraft, and A321XLRs will be taking over the transcon routes.

American has stopped selling first class on these planes for flights as of March 28, 2027. After that date we’ll still see some of the planes flying with the cabins, but the first class seats will simply be sold as business class.

American Airlines has officially eliminated its international first class product, as Boeing 777-300ERs no longer have Flagship First for sale. These planes are being retrofitted, as first class seats are being eliminated, and new business class suites are being introduced. However, the planes will keep flying around with the current cabins for quite some time, and business class passengers can freely assign the first class seats.

In the spring, we’ll see American eliminate its last “premium” first class product, which is the A321T first class cabin, as those planes are replaced by A321XLRs.

What do you make of the end of American’s Flagship First on the 777?

#6120. Why International First Class Has Failed At US Airlines (But Shouldn’t)

We’ve just seen American formally retire its Boeing 777 first class, and with that, no airline in the United States has a “true” international first class anymore. It’s the end of an era, because going back many decades, premium products were largely pioneered by US carriers. So I think this raises the question — why can US carriers not make first class work in a way that’s economically viable, especially as they keep talking about how premium they are?

Before we get into this, let me make sure we’re all on the same page when it comes to terms. This post isn’t about the premium cabin on domestic flights, which is often referred to as first class. Instead, it’s about international flights that have a cabin above business class, when it’s marketed as first class. So this would include airlines on my list of the world’s best first class products.

Airline executives are divided on the merits of having an international first class cabin. Some insist that there’s no need for such a cabin, as business class has improved so much. Meanwhile others absolutely see merit to such a product.

I mean, just look at how carriers like Air France, Lufthansa, Singapore Airlines, and SWISS, are all investing in first class. I think Air France’s La Premiere first class is the perfect example of the upside such a product has for an airline:

What’s interesting is that for the airlines that succeed with first class, the single biggest market — and single biggest point of sale — is the United States. So how is it that carriers like Air France, Lufthansa, SWISS, etc., can make money offering first class to the United States (primarily targeting Americans), but US airlines seemingly can’t?

The US has way too many people with tens or hundreds of millions of dollars, or even billions of dollars. There are plenty of people who would pay to fly private, and would pay for Air France La Premiere first class, but would never consider paying the high price for first class on a US carrier, because it’s just not worth it.

When they fly first class, they want this…

It’s no surprise that first class at US carriers has historically failed. In many ways, it reflects the failures of the industry from decades past. In other words, first class has long been thought of as “upgrade class,” rather than something actually worth paying for. US carriers have managed to change that narrative on domestic flights, but not so much on international flights.

What explains the failure of first class at US carriers? If you ask me, here are the main factors:

Call it a hot take, but I think international first class absolutely could succeed at a US carrier, if done right, with a couple of caveats. Let me start with the two main hurdles that would need to be overcome, and I’ll acknowledge, this might just be the biggest issue:

If those hurdles could be overcome, here’s the play, as I see it (and yes, this is largely inspired by Air France La Premiere):

I think the halo effect of something like this would be massive as well. Seriously, US airline executives love to talk about how premium they are, but they can’t even introduce a top-end product, despite having access to the most lucrative customer base in the world.

In terms of economics, let me also point out that the opportunity cost of a first class cabin isn’t actually that high. “Premium” is all the rage, so what you do here is eliminate some economy seats:

At this point, no airline from the United States offers first class on international flights anymore. For airlines that can’t stop talking about how unbelievably premium they are, I find that to be a pretty perplexing reality. I know that many people have just accepted “oh, a good business class is the future,” but I have a different take.

I think no US carrier actually being able to offer a globally competitive product is a failure in strategy and creativity. They have access to the world’s most lucrative customer base, and other airlines can seemingly make money serving US customers with a first class product. The issue is, US carriers have long not actually given people a reason to fly first class, all while offering too much capacity.

Personally I think there would be a lot of merit to an international first class product that’s boutique, and is operated in the right markets. That’s not to say that I think it’ll happen — I don’t — but I do think it could succeed. The only real hurdle to overcome would be how to ensure good service…

What’s your take on the possible merit of US carriers offering first class?

#6119. Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

The new office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

Britt, R-Ala., said the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

“This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting new technologies and gaps between sectors,” she said in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”

The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide said.

The office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

The House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

Senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring

It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

“If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

#6118. Unresponsive Cessna Prompts Air Canada Boeing 737 MAX 8 TCAS Alert Over Palm Springs

An Air Canada Boeing 737 MAX 8 received a Traffic Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) alert after encountering an unresponsive Cessna while climbing out of Palm Springs International Airport (PSP) last week. AC1769, bound for Vancouver International Airport (YVR), reportedly received a resolution advisory at approximately 11,400 feet, prompting its pilots to climb to 12,000 feet to avoid the nearby aircraft. The incident occurred shortly after the aircraft departed Palm Springs, with the smaller aircraft reportedly failing to respond.

Although the encounter triggered an automated collision-avoidance warning, the Air Canada aircraft continued its scheduled journey without diverting or returning to the airport. The 737 MAX 8 subsequently landed safely in Vancouver. While the incident highlights the importance of onboard collision-avoidance technology, several details surrounding the encounter, including the Cessna's identity and the minimum distance between the two aircraft, remain unknown.

According to AIRLIVE, AC1769 departed Palm Springs International Airport at 12:45 PM local time on November 17. The aircraft, registered C-FSDB, was a 737 MAX 8 operating a scheduled service to Vancouver. It departed from Runway 31R and began its climb towards cruising altitude when its onboard Traffic Collision Avoidance System detected potentially conflicting traffic.

The reported encounter involved a small Cessna that was not responding as the Canadian aircraft climbed through approximately 11,400 feet. The TCAS resolution advisory instructed the Air Canada pilots to climb to 12,000 feet, representing an additional 600 feet of altitude. This maneuver was intended to establish greater vertical separation between the two aircraft and resolve the potential traffic conflict.

Importantly, the reported alert was a resolution advisory (RA), not a proximity warning. According to AeroSillage, an RA provides pilots with instructions to modify or maintain their vertical flight path to address a potential collision threat. The available reports do not establish the exact distance between the aircraft when the alert occurred.

TCAS is an important layer of aviation safety, particularly when aircraft encounter potentially conflicting traffic in busy airspace. The technology uses information transmitted by nearby aircraft transponders to identify potential collision threats. Depending on the circumstances, the system can issue traffic advisories or resolution advisories, recommending that pilots climb or descend to increase vertical separation.

Unlike instructions from air traffic controllers, TCAS resolution advisories are generated automatically using onboard surveillance equipment. According to the Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Aeronautical Information Manual, pilots are expected to follow an RA promptly unless doing so would jeopardize the aircraft's safety. However, the circumstances surrounding the Cessna's reported lack of response remain unclear. AeroSillage noted that the available reporting does not establish whether the smaller aircraft failed to answer a radio communication or did not comply with an air traffic controller's instruction. Its registration, the nature of the communication attempts, and the minimum separation between the aircraft have not been disclosed.

A private aircraft made an unexpected turn, putting it on a course to collide with the inbound American Airlines aircraft.

Despite the reported encounter, AC1769 continued its journey to Canada without an emergency diversion. AIRLIVE reported that the aircraft landed at Vancouver International Airport at 4:45 PM local time, completing the approximately two-hour-and-40-minute journey. Flight-tracking information independently confirms that this 737 MAX 8 operated the Palm Springs-Vancouver service and reached its destination. No other details or further emergency involving the aircraft were reported. Nevertheless, the incident illustrates how unexpected traffic conflicts can require immediate action even during otherwise routine departures.

Based on available reporting, no specific findings from the US or Canadian authorities have established the circumstances of the encounter. Without an official reconstruction, it remains impossible to determine whether the Cessna experienced a communication problem, whether an instruction was missed, or how close the aircraft actually came.

#6117. Why I’d Pick Economy Over Premium Economy On An Overnight Flight

I just got back to Rio after a quick trip to Ireland for Aer Lingus’ event to showcase their new A330 cabins, including its first-ever premium economy.

I flew Air France economy both ways, and I’m glad I resisted the offer of $420 during online check-in to upgrade the outbound overnight economy leg. Ironically, it was the long day-flight back where I actually wished I’d upgraded.

However, to answer the economy vs. premium economy question, it all comes down to maximising comfort, and I think this is easier to do in economy than premium economy.

If, like me, sleeping upright or on your back is almost impossible, then what follows will likely apply to you.

The main reason I’m deterred to pick premium economy for overnight flights is because of the fixed armrests, where tray tables are sometimes stowed in this cabin.

Despite the extra recline and leg rest element (which sometimes makes it even harder to get comfortable), the fixed armrests restrict the ability to sleep any way other than straight like a pencil.

To make matters worse, they stop you from lying across more than one seat if you find yourself in an empty row.

It’s for that reason that I much prefer economy. While having a row to yourself isn’t guaranteed, there’s at least a chance of being able to move around the cabin, or stretch out into an empty seat. No matter where you sit or how empty the cabin is, you can’t do that in premium economy.

Another element of my pre-trip planning that I expect many of you to relate to is the fact it takes me so long umming and aahing over the best seat to pick.

Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status (SkyTeam Elite Plus), I could pick any seat in the economy cabin of the Boeing 777-200ER for free from 72 hours before departure.

I narrowed it down to an empty seat in the exit row, and the only row of three with an empty middle seat. I didn’t even consider one of the many empty middle rows of four seats in case they filled up before take off and I ended up in an aisle with no window to rest my head. Using the window or plane’s fuselage to rest my head on is the only saving grace for me when trying to sleep sitting upright.

As the empty exit seat would have the same restricting fixed partition as premium, I decided against that, too.

After the “boarding complete” announcement was made, the middle seat in my row remained empty, and there were three seats free in the middle of row 25, a row in front. I explained to the girl in the aisle seat that if one of us moved to the other row, we’d both have three seats to ourselves. She didn’t seem to understand my point, and said she’d prefer to sit in the aisle than us both have three free seats to ourselves.

I didn’t want to move to the middle seats either, so I got as comfortable as I could using the middle seat and the pillow I brought from home.

In the end, I did manage to get some half decent curled up shut eye (the thick pillow protected my back from the hard parts of the seat when propped against the fuselage). However, when I went to the loo, I noticed some people in the rear cabin had got lucky and were fast asleep spread across a whole four seats.

Maybe I’ll take more of a risk next time…

I’m not saying economy is always a better choice than premium. For example, I’d always recommend Emirates’ pretty darn impressive premium economy over economy, because it genuinely is several steps up from economy.

If it was up to me, I’d have had a lie-flat seat for the overnight segment. I didn’t, and I’m pretty certain I got better sleep quality curled up across two seats in economy that I would have almost upright on my back in premium.

Would you ever choose economy over premium economy?

The Centurion Card from American Express has a reputation that few other cards can match. Its invitation-only application process, substantial fees and long list of perks have made the Amex “Black Card” a status symbol.

But you don't need a Centurion invitation to get better treatment at a hotel, airport lounge access or have someone help with a dinner reservation. Plenty of cards offer those benefits, often for a fraction of the cost.

Some Centurion perks remain difficult to replicate. Others are available with cards you might already have — and, in a few cases, another card can get you a higher level of status.

Here's what to know about the U.S. Centurion Card and the other ways to get its most useful benefits.

The information for the Centurion Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

There are personal and business versions of the Centurion Card. Both are invitation-only.

Amex doesn't publish a spending threshold that guarantees an invitation. Reports of the amounts required vary widely, and meeting a rumored minimum doesn't mean you'll be invited to apply.

If you're interested, you can contact Amex to ask about consideration. Just don't build your spending strategy around getting an invitation: There isn't a published qualification path you can follow as you would for airline or hotel elite status.

The has an $895 annual fee (see rates and fees). That's a substantial expense, but the Centurion Card costs considerably more.

The Centurion Card carries a $10,000 initiation fee and a $5,000 annual fee, bringing the first-year tab to $15,000 between the two.

At that price, the card needs to do considerably more than earn rewards. Whether it makes sense will depend on how much you use its services and benefits and how much you'd otherwise pay for them.

Related: Is the Amex Platinum worth its annual fee?

The Centurion Card has some impressive benefits, but its base earning rate of 1 Membership Rewards point per dollar spent isn't a reason to get it. The business version has additional earning opportunities, including a 1.5-point rate on eligible large purchases.

Other options for earning: You'll generally get better Membership Rewards point-earning potential in bonus categories with the or the .

For example, the Platinum earns 5 points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with airlines or through American Express Travel® (on up to $500,000 of those purchases per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar spent).

And if you aren't loyal to Membership Rewards, the (see rates and fees) earns 4 Chase Ultimate Rewards points per dollar spent on flights and hotels booked directly and 3 points per dollar spent on dining. The Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card earns at least 2 miles per dollar spent on all purchases.

Along with being a status marker itself, the Centurion Card offers complimentary elite status with several loyalty programs.

Marriott Bonvoy Gold elite status includes a 25% bonus on eligible base points, a welcome gift (at participating brands), space-available room upgrades and 2 p.m. late checkout (when available). It doesn't include complimentary breakfast or lounge access.

Other ways to get it: The and (with a $895 annual fee; see rates and fees) offer Gold status (enrollment required).

The , Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful® Credit Card and also provide automatic Gold status.

The provides the higher Platinum Elite tier automatically.

The information for the Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Hilton Honors Diamond status includes a 100% bonus on eligible base points, executive lounge access (at properties with an eligible lounge) and space-available upgrades (that can include suites). Breakfast or food-and-beverage benefits vary by brand and region.

Although Diamond was once Hilton's highest elite tier, the program introduced Diamond Reserve in 2026. Still, Diamond remains valuable for frequent Hilton guests, particularly those staying at full-service properties.

Other ways to get it: You can get Diamond automatically by holding the , which has a $550 annual fee (see rates and fees).

Alternatively, you can earn it (through the end of the following calendar year) by spending $40,000 in a calendar year on the or the .

Centurion cardmembers can enroll for IHG One Rewards Diamond Elite status. Benefits include a 100% bonus on eligible base points, space-available upgrades and the option to choose breakfast for two as a welcome amenity (at participating brands). Diamond doesn't automatically include club lounge access.

Other ways to get it: You can earn Diamond Elite status by meeting these calendar-year spending requirements:

Platinum Medallion status offers eligible complimentary upgrades, priority airport services and 9 miles per dollar on eligible Delta-marketed flights.

Other ways to get it: There isn't a comparable automatic Platinum status benefit on a widely available U.S. credit card. However, you can fast-track your path with the , , or .

Each card provides 2,500 Medallion Qualification Dollars annually through MQD Headstart.

Both the Reserve and Business Reserve have a $650 annual fee (see rates and fees and rates and fees, respectively) and earn 1 MQD per $10 in eligible purchases, while the Platinum cards earn 1 MQD per $20.

Hertz Platinum offers benefits beyond the rental company's publicly earned tiers, including delivery services (at participating locations), and complimentary child seats and ski racks.

Other ways to get it: Hertz President’s Circle status is a more accessible alternative, although it isn't the same tier. It offers benefits such as vehicle upgrades (at participating locations) and a higher earning rate on eligible rentals.

You can enroll with the , , Venture X*, Capital One Venture X Business* and the Delta Reserve personal and business cards. U.S. consumer and business Platinum cardmembers who enrolled before July 9, 2026, must re-enroll through the Car Rental Privileges tile in their Amex benefits by Dec. 31, 2026. Avis President's Club offers space-available double upgrades (on eligible reservations) and guaranteed availability of a car (up to full size with a confirmed reservation made at least 24 hours ahead).

Centurion enhancements at participating properties include an additional $200 credit (on stays of at least two consecutive nights; book by phone through Centurion services).

There are also comparable hotel programs outside Amex. The and offer The Edit; the Venture X and Capital One Venture X Business offer the Premier Collection; and those with the (see rates and fees) and (see rates and fees) can book The Reserve by Citi Travel.

Eligible bookings can include breakfast for two, a $100 property credit and space-available room upgrades. Their rules differ — particularly around late checkout — so compare the benefits and total price before booking.

Related: A comparison of luxury hotel programs from credit card issuers

One of the Centurion Card's most appealing services is its concierge, which can help with requests such as restaurant reservations, event tickets and travel arrangements. How much that's worth depends on how often you use it and the assistance you receive.

Here’s what the original Points Guy himself, Brian Kelly, has to say about Ray, his Centurion concierge:

I’d guess that Ray saves me more than $20,000 a year. From knowing my preferred seat on a plane based on the layout of the cabin to advising hotels of my arrival and departure time, Ray is a jack of all trades. He’s arranged a tour in Beijing for me and my parents to visit the Forbidden City, Tiananmen Square and the Great Wall of China. He’s gotten me theater tickets, great concert seats (front row for Celine Dion) and hard-to-get restaurant reservations. Ray even takes on particularly cumbersome tasks, like locating my headphones when I lost them 10,000 miles from home.

Centurion† assistance at participating airports requires a first- or business-class ticket paid with the card through Amex Travel (and a request at least 74 hours ahead). Availability applies; expedited immigration isn't guaranteed.

Other ways to get it: You can purchase airport meet-and-greet services separately. That can be worth comparing if you need assistance on a particular trip, although you'll need to pay for the service yourself.

Centurion cardmembers receive access to Amex’s Global Lounge Collection, including Centurion Lounges, Priority Pass lounges (enrollment required), Escape Lounges, Plaza Premium lounges, Lufthansa lounges and Delta Sky Clubs.

Guest rules depend on the lounge. At U.S. Centurion Lounges and select international locations, Centurion cardmembers can bring their immediate family — a spouse or domestic partner and children under 18 — or up to two guests without charge. Delta Sky Club guests generally cost $50 each.

Centurion cardmembers also have access to reserved seating or dedicated spaces at select Centurion Lounges. Some locations go further: Tokyo Haneda Airport (HND) has a Centurion-only room with its own beverage station.

Other ways to get it: The and are the closest alternatives for access to the same lounge networks (enrollment may be required), with stricter visit and guest rules. Each provides 10 Delta Sky Club Visits per Medallion Year on eligible travel, compared with Centurion's unlimited eligible visits. Platinum cardmembers generally pay for Centurion Lounge guests unless they meet the $75,000 annual spending requirement for complimentary guest access.

The Delta Reserve personal and business cards offer 15 Sky Club Visits per Medallion Year and Centurion Lounge access on eligible Delta itineraries. Both those cards and the Amex Platinum cards can unlock unlimited Sky Club visits after $75,000 in eligible calendar-year purchases.

For lounge access outside Amex, the and offer Sapphire and Priority Pass lounge access, while the offers Priority Pass and four Admirals Club passes per calendar year. The Venture X and Venture X Business offer Capital One Lounges and Landings plus Priority Pass. None of these cards provides Centurion Lounge access.

The Centurion Card includes a PS membership and two complimentary Salon visits with a guest per calendar year (booked through Centurion services; after enrollment). The Salon is a shared lounge experience, distinct from a private suite.

PS operates at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW), Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and Miami International Airport (MIA).

Other ways to get it: You can book PS without a special credit card or a membership. Nonmember rates start at $1,295 per person for the Salon and $4,950 one-way for a private suite for up to four travelers (excluding taxes and fees).

Centurion cardmembers enjoy the highest level of travel and shopping protections American Express has to offer, including protection against trip delay and cancellation** and baggage delays*** as well as extended warranty*** and purchase protection.***

Other ways to get it: The and offer several overlapping protections; similar protections can be found on many cards across Amex’s portfolio.

**Eligibility and benefit level vary by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for details. Policies are underwritten by New Hampshire Insurance Company, an AIG Company.

**Eligibility and benefit level vary by card. Terms, conditions and limitations apply. Visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for details. Policies are underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

Centurion cardmembers receive access to dining opportunities and special events. However, several useful reservation benefits are available with less exclusive cards.

The Centurion Card combines some hard-to-replicate services with benefits you can get elsewhere.

If Hilton Diamond status is what matters to you, the is a straightforward alternative. If you want Marriott status, the actually provides a higher tier. And for lounge access and hotel booking perks, the and cover much of the same ground.

Ultimately, the Centurion Card's biggest differentiators are its exclusive experiences and personalized services. If those aren't priorities, you may be able to get the benefits you value most from a far less expensive card.

Start with the benefits you'll use, then work out which card provides them at a cost you can justify. You might not need an invitation to make your next trip more comfortable.

#6114. Third Time’s Not The Charm: A SWISS A220’s Odd Triple Aborted Takeoff

If you’re a frequent flyer, odds are that you’ve encountered an aborted takeoff, whereby the plane accelerates down the runway, only to slow down, and eventually come to a stop. In some cases this can feel like a non-event, while in other cases it can feel much scarier, depending on the speed at which the takeoff is aborted.

However, here’s something you don’t often see — a SWISS Airbus A220 aborted its takeoff three times in a row, before finally returning to the gate to see what was going on, as reported by Blick. The explanation is actually quite logical, but that doesn’t make the whole ordeal any less unusual.

On Tuesday, November 17, 2026, SWISS flight LX2110 was scheduled to operate from Zurich (ZRH) to Malaga (AGP), with a 9:35AM departure. The flight was operated by an Airbus A220-300 with the registration code HB-JCM.

The plane pushed back and taxied out to the runway right on schedule. The pilots began the takeoff roll, but then quickly applied the brakes, causing the plane to come to a stop, while still at a slow speed. The pilots took a moment to run checklists, and then decided on another takeoff attempt, only for the same thing to happen again!

After the second aborted takeoff, the captain reportedly informed passengers that the thrust levers had popped out during the takeoff roll, and that was the reason for the aborted takeoff. However, rather than returning to the gate, they decided to attempt an additional takeoff roll.

Once again, the takeoff was aborted. At that point the captain explained that nothing like this had ever happened to him before in his 12 year career, and that the plane would be returning to the gate.

There ended up being a plane change, and then the A220 with the registration code HB-JCO was assigned to operate this flight — it ended up taking off at 1:29PM and landing at 3:52PM, around 3.5 hours behind schedule.

A SWISS spokesperson confirmed the incident happened, though noted that the takeoffs were aborted at a low speed of around 50 kilometers per hour (around 30 miles per hour).

What explains the aborted takeoffs? Well, it was because as the plane accelerated for takeoff, the automatic thrust control system automatically deactivated. To explain this as simply as possible, as I understand it, on the A220 when the auto-thrust is armed and the thrust levers are moved forward for takeoff, the auto-thrust then takes over, and moves the levers forward without manual intervention.

In other words, one of the pilots keeps their hands on the auto-thrust levers and “moves” with them, but doesn’t actually apply any force. Pilots are trained this way, and to not manually apply force. In the event that the crew tries to stop the auto-thrust lever motion, a pressure switch detects this, and then disengages the auto-thrust, to allow for a manual override.

In this case, the auto-thrust incorrectly detected resistance, when the pilots weren’t attempting to apply it. According to the airline, the system that monitors the aircraft’s technical status in real time was unable to identify the cause of the error, as no errors were displayed in the system. So at first, the pilots likely wondered if they had accidentally applied force.

However, once technicians had a look at the plane, it was discovered that the switch for disabling the automatic thrust control on the original aircraft was stuck, and this caused the automatic thrust control to shut down during takeoff attempts.

So while this can understandably seem scary to passengers, this wasn’t even a direct safety issue. After all, the pilots could’ve also manually moved the throttles. However, you also don’t want to take off when you know there’s an issue with the throttles, since that’s not exactly a best practice.

A SWISS Airbus A220 attempted a takeoff from Zurich three times in a row. While I’ve had two consecutive aborted takeoffs, I’ve never had three, and I can’t imagine that happens all too often.

While this is unusual, it sounds like this was handled well, and I can see why the pilots kept trying. This wasn’t a critical safety issue, but instead, just an incorrect detection of inputs, in a way that wouldn’t really pose a risk to the flight. At the same time, you don’t want to knowingly take off with a fault switch.

What do you make of this SWISS aborted takeoff trio?

#6113. Mexico’s President Flew 21 Hours To China In Economy (In A Middle Seat!)

I’ve gotta say, huge kudos to Mexico’s President, Claudia Sheinbaum, for setting quite the example in terms of how she recently traveled to China, as flagged by View from the Wing…

World leaders have just met in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting. As you’d expect, most leaders flew on their government planes. There were some exceptions, though I can’t imagine anyone else flew the same way as Mexico’s 64-year-old president.

Viajamos hacia Shenzhen para representar a México en el Foro de Cooperación Económica Asia-Pacífico (APEC) China 2026; la agenda de actividades incluye reunión con empresarios de países miembros. Además, participaré en la conferencia de prensa matutina para informar avances de… pic.twitter.com/F9UqRLjFlb

Media reports suggest she flew to China on China Southern. Specifically, she traveled on Sunday, November 15, 2026, on CZ8032, from Mexico City (MEX) to Shenzhen (SZX), with a refueling stop in Tijuana (TIJ), and the journey covering a distance of 8,803 miles.

The Airbus A350-900 took off from Mexico City at 12:49AM, arriving in Tijuana at 2:02AM, after a flight time of 3hr13min. Then it took off again at 4:34AM, and landed in Shenzhen the following morning at 11:31AM, after a flight time of 14hr56min. All-in-all, the flight took around 21 hours, including the refueling stop.

The shocking thing here isn’t that she traveled commercial, but instead, that she reportedly flew in economy! Reports suggest she was in seat 33B, which would be a middle seat in economy, no less!

Llegamos a la Ciudad de México en el vuelo CZ8031 desde Shenzhen, China. Agradecemos a toda la tripulación por su apoyo. pic.twitter.com/DSC83CpnDQ

I think a head of state should reasonably be able to fly business class on a flight of this length, for two reasons:

That being said, I absolutely commend her for the example she is setting. It’s certainly quite a contrast to what we’ve seen here, where President Trump accepted a Boeing 747-8 as a gift from Qatar, and talked about how he has done it to make Americans be proud, because “our country has to be represented properly.” Heck, just this week he talked about “China was very impressed” and “Russia was very impressed” of his new plane. Lovely, I’m happy we’re impressing Putin, that makes me proud to be an American!

"Russia was very impressed" — Trump leads his press conference by bragging about taking the longest flight in Air Force One history, in case you were worried that he actually accomplished something useful on his trip pic.twitter.com/dDIHg8wb1w

Keep in mind that Mexico has an interesting history when it comes to how leaders fly. In 2016, Mexico’s government took control of a private Boeing 787, which flew around former President Enrique Pena Nieto. The purchase of the plane had actually been arranged under the previous president, Felipe Calderón, in 2012.

Then in 2018, when Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador took charge in Mexico, he fulfilled a campaign promise of selling that 787, which turned out to be pretty challenging, given that demand for a secondhand VIP 787 isn’t exactly that high (the plane ended up going to Tajikistan). Sheinbaum has kept that general legacy going, by flying commercial.

Mexico’s President, Claudia Sheinbaum, traveled to the recent summit in China differently than virtually all other government leaders. Not only did she fly commercial, but she traveled in economy, and reportedly even in a middle seat.

There’s no denying that this is more about optics than anything, but I very much respect that. It’s nice to see heads of state who lead by example, as it’s pretty rare to see nowadays.

What do you make of Sheinbaum’s travel style?

#6112. Democrats nominate Jeffries to be House speaker, a historic first

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no announced opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

“It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries said at a press conference following the election.

While Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

“Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get big things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”

Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”

Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

“This is the beginning of a new bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., said at the press conference.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

Jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the new majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

At his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

“We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

“I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”

Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had said they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

Pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

The entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

Jeffries said Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”

Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

“House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he said at his news conference.

#6111. The Aircraft Set To Replace British Airways’ Boeing 777-200ERs At London Heathrow

British Airways (BA) is about to retire the aircraft that built its long-haul network, but it has not told anyone exactly what will take its place at London Heathrow (LHR). The airline’s 43 Boeing 777-200ERs average roughly 26 years of age, according to Aerospace Global News, and most of them fly from Heathrow rather than Gatwick. The one firm date BA has given belongs to the other London airport: in a February 27, 2026 message to colleagues, CEO Sean Doyle said the first new Boeing 787-10 will be delivered to Gatwick in 2029, as published by the British Airways Media Centre.

So what is actually coming for Heathrow’s 777-200ERs? Two types dominate the picture: the Airbus A350-1000, which is already stepping onto some of that flying, and the Boeing 787-10, with the long-delayed Boeing 777-9 expected to follow. One caveat before going further. BA has published neither a retirement date nor a route-by-route replacement plan for Heathrow, so every swap beyond Nashville described below is a possibility. The first real clue, though, arrived from the home of country music, and it hints at a bigger shift than a simple like-for-like swap. Read on, because the answer may change which jet you board on your next transatlantic trip.

Gatwick (LGW) is the easiest part of the puzzle to understand because BA has actually given it a delivery date. Aerospace Global News, citing Cirium data, reported that BA served 13 destinations from Gatwick in March 2026, all lower-yielding leisure flights, from Antigua and Cancun to Orlando and Mauritius, plus Accra and Islamabad for visiting-friends-and-relatives traffic. The same outlet notes that around 12 aircraft are typically based there and that some suggest 17 could be once the 787-10 arrives. The new jets are not expected to have a First cabin. The outlet also suggests that a larger Gatwick presence could make the airport more attractive to oneworld partner airlines hoping to feed connecting passengers into BA’s network.

There is also a technical twist. According to Turning Left For Less, BA’s earliest 787-10s lacked crew rest bunks and were range-limited, so the newly ordered aircraft will get an increased-gross-weight modification and bunks. The site lists Vancouver, Phoenix, Mauritius, Cancun and Las Vegas as routes that become workable. BA's newly ordered Boeing 787-10s will be powered by General Electric GEnx engines, following the airline's decision to introduce a second engine supplier alongside Rolls-Royce on its Dreamliner fleet. Doyle’s own message confirmed the bunks, and Aerospace Global News adds that the rest areas should be welcome news for crew, since the airline’s initial 787-10s do not have them.

That gives BA a relatively clean renewal path at LGW. Heathrow is harder. Most of the 43 777-200ERs are still tied to the airport, and replacing a four-class, business-heavy aircraft with a 787-10 without First would change the product as well as the capacity. Yet one Heathrow route has already provided a much more interesting clue.

The Airbus A350-1000 is not merely a future possibility at Heathrow. As reported by Simple Flying, BA scheduled the A350-1000 to replace the 777-200ER on its daily Heathrow–Nashville service from March 29, based on schedule data first spotted by Ishrion Aviation. Published flight times stay at 9 hours 10 minutes outbound as BA223 and 8 hours 10 minutes back as BA222, although the A350 cruises slightly faster than the 777. In winter, the route has used the Boeing 787-8, and the report says there is no word yet on whether that aircraft returns once the cold season arrives.

Simple Flying's database shows the Heathrow 777-200ER on this route seats 272 passengers, while the A350-1000 seats 331, a jump of 59. The seat models are the same, but Simple Flying notes BA fits a smaller galley area to squeeze in the extra rows, and Turning Left For Less says cabin crew have voiced concern about galley space on the type.

Seat counts on Heathrow–Nashville, per aeroLOPA data cited by Simple Flying.

Economy passengers may even gain a little comfort, since the A350 has one fewer seat per row than the 777. But the strategic point is bigger: BA added 59 seats to a route without adding a single flight. Why would an airline do that, and what does it say about the rest of Heathrow’s fleet? There is also a cargo angle. Simple Flying points out that the A350-1000 is comparable in size to the Boeing 777-300ER and so has a significantly larger hold, which on a short transatlantic sector lets BA load more freight than before.

A look at the changes coming to this route and what it means.

Because Heathrow is the one airport where BA cannot simply add flights. Writing in 2023, when the airline was still weighing its options, One Mile At A Time argued that Heathrow is capacity-controlled and that the larger A350-1000 and 787–10 variants offer excellent economics. They also noted that BA’s 777 fleet averaged nearly 20 years of age at the time, with nearly two-thirds of the jets delivered in 2001 or earlier, mostly the 777-200ER variant. Aerospace Global News makes a similar point about Gatwick: basing new jets there relieves pressure on a heavily slot-constrained Heathrow hub.

Efficiency is the other half of the logic. According to Airbus, the A350 Family delivers a 25% advantage in fuel burn, operating costs and CO₂ emissions compared with previous-generation competitor aircraft. That improvement comes from combining advanced aerodynamics, new-generation Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engines and lightweight materials, which account for more than 70% of the airframe. For BA, this makes the A350-1000 particularly attractive at a slot-constrained airport such as Heathrow: it can carry more passengers on an existing departure while benefiting from the efficiency gains of a newer-generation design.

That combination of capacity and efficiency helps explain why BA has ordered more than one type of new-generation widebody rather than choosing a single replacement for every 777. The order book tells the story. BA has 24 Boeing 777-9s on order after adding six aircraft in March 2025. It has also ordered six additional A350-1000s and 38 Boeing 787-10s, including the 32-aircraft order announced in 2025.

Those numbers make one aircraft particularly important. Twenty-four 777-9s are supposed to become BA's largest new-generation widebodies, but none has yet joined the fleet. The timing of that arrival could determine how quickly the oldest Heathrow 777s can finally disappear.

The 777-9 is the biggest aircraft in BA's replacement plan, and it is also the one that introduces the most uncertainty. We reported in August 2026 that the aircraft was still working through the tail end of its certification sequence as of mid-2026. In a November piece, we added that Boeing is expected to deliver its first 777-9 in 2027, by which time Airbus will likely have well over 150 A350-1000s flying.

For BA, Turning Left For Less expects a four-class layout of eight First, 65 Club Suites, 46 World Traveller Plus and 206 economy seats, 325 in all, debuting from 2027 or 2028 with the airline’s new First suite. Against the A350-1000’s 331 seats, the 777-9 would not even add capacity on a Nashville-type route, which complicates the idea of the 777-9 as a simple 777-200ER successor.

The same site expects the new First suite to be limited to the 24 Boeing 777-9s and the 12 refurbished Airbus A380s, which would make the 777-9 as much a flagship statement as a fleet-replacement tool.

Until the 777-9 shows up, the old jets keep flying, and flying hard, with most replacements still years away. What does that wait mean for passengers boarding one tomorrow?

Ten classic airliners relied on a third cockpit crew member, but their reasons for doing so reveal how dramatically commercial aviation evolved.

That leaves BA with an awkward transition period. Turning Left For Less says BA intends to retire all 43 777-200ERs, some of which will exceed 30 years of age by withdrawal, and its reader analysis suggests the last four, delivered in 2009, could stay longer because they are younger. BA has confirmed none of that beyond Doyle’s statement about Gatwick. Put differently, the exit date for the oldest airframes is still a matter of informed speculation, not a published schedule.

The wait has had visible moments. FlyMag reported that BA229 to Baltimore returned to Heathrow on July 9, 2026, and BA183 to New York turned back the next evening, both operated by 777-200ERs after crews identified technical issues, and both flights were subsequently canceled. Age alone is not proof of unreliability, since many 777s worldwide have flown happily for decades, but the incidents landed just as the renewal timeline moved into focus.

Every extra month of waiting sharpens the question BA has so far left unanswered in public: which Heathrow route loses its 777-200ER next, and will passengers on it get a First cabin back? The answer may arrive route by route, in schedule filings, long before any formal announcement.

Two milestones will settle how this plays out, and neither is fully in BA’s hands. The first is the pace of 787-10 deliveries after the Gatwick debut in 2029. The second is whether Boeing can certify and hand over the 777-9 on the schedule it now promises. If the Dreamliners flow, BA can retire 777-200ERs without leaving Heathrow gaps. If the 777-9 slips again, the A350-1000 is the obvious stopgap, yet the six additional aircraft on order are a modest cushion.

There is a premium-cabin cost to watch as well. Turning Left For Less points out that the new First suite does not fit four abreast in a 787 and that the A350-1000 carries no First at all, so some Heathrow routes could lose the cabin entirely as the 777-200ERs go. That is precisely the trade-off BA has not yet explained to the customers paying for it. Some will welcome newer jets with quieter cabins and more consistent Club Suites; others will see a quiet downgrade of the flagship experience at the airport where BA charges its highest fares.

One Mile At A Time wrote a 2023 article saying they were curious about how it would all play out. Three years on, the cast is clear, but the final act is not. So what do you think: should BA hold on to its youngest 777-200ERs until the 777-9 arrives, or are the A350-1000 and 787-10 enough on their own? Tell us in the comments, and let us know which Heathrow route you would like to see upgraded first.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Those who were first class passengers two decades ago are now flying private.
