#6052. Appeals court stands by LaMonica McIver ruling

Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.

The decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit leaves in place a 2-1 opinion from August which held that McIver was not immune from the charges, which stemmed from a confrontation between visiting members of Congress and federal agents while at the Delaney Hall facility in Newark. McIver has challenged the charges, arguing that her visit fell under the “speech or debate” immunity she has as a member of Congress because she was there to inspect detention conditions.

In a statement McIver said she and her attorneys were looking at “every possible option” in response to the appeals court ruling. Her statement invoked the Trump administration’s threats to treat oversight efforts as criminal conduct and said “we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.”

“Donald Trump continues to send warning shots to Democrats in Congress and in all levels of power — but their case against me right now, in broad daylight, goes well beyond a warning. Because of a weaponized Department of Justice and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver said in her statement.

Following Thursday’s decision on rehearing, McIver could next ask the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case.

The August majority opinion from Judge Cindy Chung, which Thursday’s decision leaves in place, said that two of the three charges against McIver did not fall under the immunity, which is limited to legislative acts. The majority sent the third charge back to the lower court for another ruling.

“We have considered the ‘nature’ of the charged conduct and concluded it is unambiguously non-legislative,” the judge wrote.

Separately, Judge Thomas Ambro partially dissented to offer a different approach to the case. Ambro would have required the trial judge to more closely examine the exact conduct McIver was charged with, as well as to examine whether the Trump administration targeted her because of her political views.

“I would allow her discovery into the truth of the matter — not only for her own sake but to safeguard the independence of our legislative bodies,” Ambro wrote.

Ambro did not vote on whether the full 3rd Circuit should rehear the case. Three judges voted to have the full 3rd Circuit hear McIver’s case, and Judge Emil Bove, a former Trump administration official and former personal attorney for the president, did not participate in the vote.

The criminal case started shortly after the Delaney Hall visit in May 2025, as prosecutors alleged that McIver assaulted federal agents during a scuffle around Newark Mayor Ras Baraka. Officials arrested Baraka that day and charged him with trespassing, but later dropped those charges

Court filings in the case alleged that McIver struck agents during the confrontation. McIver has argued that she was effectively being charged for doing her job and federal agents were interfering with her attempts to inspect the facility.

Earlier this year, Judge Jamel K. Semper of the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey disagreed and ruled that the case could move forward.

#6051. The Filibuster Is a Pillar of American Government

If the filibuster dies, it clears the path for sweeping changes from which American government as we know it may never recover.

About to take control of the U.S. Senate with a robust 56 seats, Democrats are now debating whether to eliminate the filibuster and change the nature of the institution forever.

Rich Lowry is the editor in chief of National Review.

#6049. Hyatt Keeps Pepsi For 10 More Years At 700+ U.S. Hotels—Even Though Few Guests Want It

Hyatt has signed up for another 10 years with Pepsi, covering more than 700 U.S. hotels. After Marriott finally decided to switch to Coca-Cola, Hyatt is sticking with the beverage that prompts a question nobody wants to hear: Is Pepsi okay? No, it isn’t. I rarely drink soda. When I do, I don’t want to waste it on Pepsi. The renewal announced November 19, flagged by The Bulkhead Seat, doesn’t cover every Hyatt brand or every country. But the economics of choosing Pepsi make more sense once you realize that the person negotiating the contract isn’t the one that has to drink it. Which Hyatt Brands Are Covered, And Where Can You Get Coke? The agreement covers U.S. hotels in Hyatt’s Classics and Essentials portfolios. Translating Hyatt’s brand groupings: Portfolio Brands Classics Grand Hyatt, Hyatt Regency, Destination by Hyatt, Hyatt Centric, Hyatt Vacation Club, Hyatt Essentials Hyatt Place, Hyatt House, Hyatt Studios, Hyatt Select, Caption by Hyatt, Unscripted by Hyatt UrCove also belongs to Essentials, but its Chinese hotels aren’t covered by a U.S. agreement. The Luxury, Lifestyle and Inclusive Collection portfolios aren’t part of this deal. No one wants to show up at an Andaz or Park Hyatt and get told they can’t have a Coke. Alila, Thompson, The Standard, and Hyatt Ziva and Zilara are also outside the deal’s scope. Here are some hotels that have specifically listed Coke: Hotel Coca-Cola On The Menu Park Hyatt New York Room service lists Coke and Diet Coke Andaz Maui Meeting and event menus list Coke and Diet Coke Thompson Dallas Room service lists Coke and Diet Coke Alila Marea Beach Resort Encinitas Room service lists bottled Coke Pepsi Doesn’t Have To Be Your First Choice To Win The Business When I covered Marriott’s switch in April, Marriott told hotels that more than 70% of its guests favored the Coca-Cola portfolio. Hotels choose suppliers based on the total deal: product pricing, rebates, equipment, servicing, marketing support and sometimes direct payments. We can see how this works in a public contract. Fresno, California’s 2018 Pepsi agreement for its convention center offered a $20,000 annual sponsorship payment, a 25% vending commission, $3 rebates per case or gallon sold, bulk pricing and equipment maintenance in exchange for exclusive beverage rights. A hotel has a modestly captive audience. You’ve already booked the room, your conference is downstairs, or you’re sitting by the pool. You can buy a Coke elsewhere, but that takes effort. Some people accept Pepsi. Others choose something else. The hotel loses some beverage sales and creates some disappointment. But it still thinks it can come out ahead if its supplier prices and rebates are better and they aren’t seeing guests change their hotel bookings. In other words, the worse product can be more profitable to the hotel – or at least to Hyatt corporate. Here, Hyatt brings access to guests whose hotel decision usually turns on something other than soda. Pepsi doesn’t have to persuade all those guests that it tastes better (it doesn’t). Getting its products stocked on property can shift purchases without changing anyone’s preferences. PepsiCo also brings Gatorade, Starbucks ready-to-drink coffee, Quaker, Lay’s, Doritos, Muscle Milk and poppi. “Is Pepsi Okay?” Was Never A Compliment The question assumes you’ve requested something else and asks whether you’ll accept a substitute you didn’t want. Pepsi understood the problem well enough to build its 2019 Super Bowl commercial around it, recruiting Steve Carell, Cardi B and Lil Jon to insist Pepsi was “More Than OK.” John Belushi’s Olympia Restaurant on Saturday Night Live had already reduced the experience to “No Coke! Pepsi!” You could order what you wanted. You were getting what the restaurant had decided to sell. The Pepsi Challenge, New Coke, And What A Recipe Can’t Copy I remember the Pepsi Challenge as a kid. I remember how scared Coke seemed, and the debacle of New Coke. The explanation popularized by Malcolm Gladwell in Blink is that Pepsi’s sweetness does better in a sip test than when someone drinks a whole can. Maybe some people really did prefer the first sip of Pepsi and then found the rest too much. That never seemed right to me. The first sip of Coke is much better. Fortunately, there’s no rule you have to finish a soda. Coca-Cola’s history of New Coke says the company’s lead over its chief competitor had been slipping for 15 consecutive years. It introduced the reformulated drink on April 23, 1985, after taste tests involving nearly 200,000 consumers favored the new formula. The original came back just 79 days later. The tests hadn’t captured how people would react to having their Coke taken away. The company could produce a drink that performed better in a test and still make customers furious by replacing the one they loved. That helps explain why Coke’s business is so hard to recreate even if someone could duplicate the liquid. The secret formula gets the attention, but a competitor would also need to reproduce decades of habits, memories, advertising and confidence that the drink will be what you expect. A familiar brand changes the experience of drinking it. Then there’s the distribution system: bottlers, delivery routes, coolers, fountains and relationships with stores and restaurants. Being easy to find reinforces the habit of asking for Coke. You know there’s already a strong likelihood it’ll be there when you ask. I don’t ask for my preferred drinks outside of places I know it’s available. Would you ask for Golden Elephant Three Lotus Pure Palm Juice at a diner off the New Jersey Turnpike? I don’t drink enough soda to make defending Coke a daily activity. If I’m going to have soda, Dr. Brown’s cream is my first choice, followed by their black cherry. Hyatt can negotiate all the Pepsi it wants. I’ll just have water, thanks. When I covered Marriott’s switch in April, Marriott told hotels that more than 70% of its guests favored the Coca-Cola portfolio.

Hotels choose suppliers based on the total deal: product pricing, rebates, equipment, servicing, marketing support and sometimes direct payments. We can see how this works in a public contract. Fresno, California’s 2018 Pepsi agreement for its convention center offered a $20,000 annual sponsorship payment, a 25% vending commission, $3 rebates per case or gallon sold, bulk pricing and equipment maintenance in exchange for exclusive beverage rights.

A hotel has a modestly captive audience. You’ve already booked the room, your conference is downstairs, or you’re sitting by the pool. You can buy a Coke elsewhere, but that takes effort. Some people accept Pepsi. Others choose something else. The hotel loses some beverage sales and creates some disappointment. But it still thinks it can come out ahead if its supplier prices and rebates are better and they aren’t seeing guests change their hotel bookings. In other words, the worse product can be more profitable to the hotel – or at least to Hyatt corporate.

Here, Hyatt brings access to guests whose hotel decision usually turns on something other than soda. Pepsi doesn’t have to persuade all those guests that it tastes better (it doesn’t). Getting its products stocked on property can shift purchases without changing anyone’s preferences. PepsiCo also brings Gatorade, Starbucks ready-to-drink coffee, Quaker, Lay’s, Doritos, Muscle Milk and poppi.

The question assumes you’ve requested something else and asks whether you’ll accept a substitute you didn’t want. Pepsi understood the problem well enough to build its 2019 Super Bowl commercial around it, recruiting Steve Carell, Cardi B and Lil Jon to insist Pepsi was “More Than OK.” John Belushi’s Olympia Restaurant on Saturday Night Live had already reduced the experience to “No Coke! Pepsi!” You could order what you wanted. You were getting what the restaurant had decided to sell. The Pepsi Challenge, New Coke, And What A Recipe Can’t Copy I remember the Pepsi Challenge as a kid. I remember how scared Coke seemed, and the debacle of New Coke. The explanation popularized by Malcolm Gladwell in Blink is that Pepsi’s sweetness does better in a sip test than when someone drinks a whole can. Maybe some people really did prefer the first sip of Pepsi and then found the rest too much. That never seemed right to me. The first sip of Coke is much better. Fortunately, there’s no rule you have to finish a soda. Coca-Cola’s history of New Coke says the company’s lead over its chief competitor had been slipping for 15 consecutive years. It introduced the reformulated drink on April 23, 1985, after taste tests involving nearly 200,000 consumers favored the new formula. The original came back just 79 days later. The tests hadn’t captured how people would react to having their Coke taken away. The company could produce a drink that performed better in a test and still make customers furious by replacing the one they loved. That helps explain why Coke’s business is so hard to recreate even if someone could duplicate the liquid. The secret formula gets the attention, but a competitor would also need to reproduce decades of habits, memories, advertising and confidence that the drink will be what you expect. A familiar brand changes the experience of drinking it. Then there’s the distribution system: bottlers, delivery routes, coolers, fountains and relationships with stores and restaurants. Being easy to find reinforces the habit of asking for Coke. You know there’s already a strong likelihood it’ll be there when you ask. I don’t ask for my preferred drinks outside of places I know it’s available. Would you ask for Golden Elephant Three Lotus Pure Palm Juice at a diner off the New Jersey Turnpike? I don’t drink enough soda to make defending Coke a daily activity. If I’m going to have soda, Dr. Brown’s cream is my first choice, followed by their black cherry. Hyatt can negotiate all the Pepsi it wants. I’ll just have water, thanks. I remember the Pepsi Challenge as a kid. I remember how scared Coke seemed, and the debacle of New Coke.

The explanation popularized by Malcolm Gladwell in Blink is that Pepsi’s sweetness does better in a sip test than when someone drinks a whole can. Maybe some people really did prefer the first sip of Pepsi and then found the rest too much. That never seemed right to me. The first sip of Coke is much better. Fortunately, there’s no rule you have to finish a soda.

Coca-Cola’s history of New Coke says the company’s lead over its chief competitor had been slipping for 15 consecutive years. It introduced the reformulated drink on April 23, 1985, after taste tests involving nearly 200,000 consumers favored the new formula. The original came back just 79 days later.

The tests hadn’t captured how people would react to having their Coke taken away. The company could produce a drink that performed better in a test and still make customers furious by replacing the one they loved.

That helps explain why Coke’s business is so hard to recreate even if someone could duplicate the liquid. The secret formula gets the attention, but a competitor would also need to reproduce decades of habits, memories, advertising and confidence that the drink will be what you expect. A familiar brand changes the experience of drinking it.

Then there’s the distribution system: bottlers, delivery routes, coolers, fountains and relationships with stores and restaurants. Being easy to find reinforces the habit of asking for Coke. You know there’s already a strong likelihood it’ll be there when you ask. I don’t ask for my preferred drinks outside of places I know it’s available. Would you ask for Golden Elephant Three Lotus Pure Palm Juice at a diner off the New Jersey Turnpike?

I don’t drink enough soda to make defending Coke a daily activity. If I’m going to have soda, Dr. Brown’s cream is my first choice, followed by their black cherry. Hyatt can negotiate all the Pepsi it wants. I’ll just have water, thanks.

#6048. United Airlines Remembers Your Bad Flight—And May Upgrade You Next Time, Even Without Status

United Airlines is giving some passengers free extra legroom on an upcoming trip because an earlier one went badly. These are passengers without elite status, and who haven’t even complained. The airline remembers the problem and offers something on its own. Aviation watchdog JonNYC shares a report from a passenger who missed a connection about a month earlier. Before their next flight, United sent a message saying they’d been moved to Economy Plus. The passenger says they have no status and the upcoming flight had a light load. The message, also covered by Paddle Your Own Kanoo, connects the better seat to the earlier experience: We know your previous travel experience may have faced some challenges JonNYC’s report on United’s next-flight Economy Plus recovery gesture — JonNYC (@xJonNYC), November 22, 2026 I like this. Airlines know when they’ve inconvenienced you. Making you write a complaint explaining something already in their records adds work to a bad experience. But the timing limits what United can accomplish: the customer already has another ticket, or buys one. This doesn’t reach someone who has no further United trip booked and refuses to buy another. This isn’t really a pure ‘win back’ effort. But this isn’t something that just started. Passengers have been reporting it since at least August 2025. Several Passenger Reports Show How This Works There are several passenger reports of this on Reddit: August 26, 2025: A Silver member reported an eight hour-plus delay leaving Denver. United gave them a $75 travel certificate, then assigned Economy Plus two days before their next flight. The seat was an additional gesture after the certificate. December 3, 2025: Another passenger the gesture after a trip with delays and seating problems. They said they hadn’t even contacted United about the previous trip. January 5, 2026: A passenger said a solo flight three weeks earlier had been delayed two hours. On the subsequent trip, both the passenger and their fiancée received Economy Plus. Jon’s example adds a customer without status, which is especially useful – United may not be using a ‘customer value score’ and limiting whom they’re reaching. And the January example suggests a companion can benefit even when they weren’t on the disrupted flight. Recipients generally appreciated being remembered. The Silver member in the August thread liked the gesture even though they expected to get Economy Plus at check-in anyway. Economy Plus is extra legroom coach. This upgrade isn’t to first class or long haul business. American Had Eagle Scores Years Ago Back in 2018, I wrote about the long-standing American Airlines Helix system and customer Eagle ratings. Those scores combined how valuable a customer was with how badly American had treated them and their risk of leaving. The one-to-five rating was recalculated daily. A high spending customer whose flights went smoothly didn’t necessarily receive the highest score. Neither did someone with terrible experiences who brought little revenue. The system helped employees decide when to make exceptions and spend more to preserve a customer relationship. One practical consequence was that customers with sufficiently high Eagle ratings could get expiring systemwide upgrades extended. Other airlines have remembered past problems, too. British Airways’ 2012 Know Me announcement described telling crew about a regular customer’s earlier weather delay so they could acknowledge it and thank the passenger for returning. Delta’s 2017 onboard recognition tool included recent flight interruptions among the reasons to flag someone for attention. British Airways and Delta were recognizing the earlier problem. United is pairing that with a better seat. United Has Been Talking About Recovery At the Barclays investor conference in February, chief financial officer Mike Leskinen discussed using technology for getting displaced crews and disrupted customers where they needed to go. And United’s Sheryl Lee described presenting Flight Finder at this year’s Grounded in Iceland conference. That tool looks for open seats for disrupted passengers already on standby. This also fits Scott Kirby’s public argument for technology that anticipates customer needs, and a pattern I’ve covered at United: making customer milestones visible to employees and offering selected travelers Global Services treatment they weren’t expecting. Airlines collect enormous amounts of customer information. The hard and useful part is actually doing something with it. But Here The Next Booking Has Already Happened The economics of this can be very good. If an Economy Plus seat would otherwise go unsold, giving it to an inconvenienced passenger costs United very little. The passenger gets something the airline normally charges for, and the message tells them why. Waiting until close to departure gives them more information about which seats they’re likely to sell. But an unannounced benefit delivered after booking can’t persuade someone to make that booking in the first place. A credit or an advance offer of a better seat can give an angry customer a reason to try the airline again. This gesture reaches people who already have another United reservation. And that doesn’t mean they’ve forgiven the airline. Their next trip could have been purchased before the bad trip. United may have the only convenient nonstop. They may be flying because their employer booked it. I especially like, though, that this can reach someone without status. An empty extra legroom seat may do more to win that customer’s business than offering the same thing to a frequent flyer who already gets it regularly. And United has to get the seat choice right. I wouldn’t consider moving from an aisle to a middle seat an improvement just because it’s in Economy Plus, and by the way United doesn’t offer free drinks in their extra legroom coach seats like even American does. This also fits Scott Kirby’s public argument for technology that anticipates customer needs, and a pattern I’ve covered at United: making customer milestones visible to employees and offering selected travelers Global Services treatment they weren’t expecting.

Airlines collect enormous amounts of customer information. The hard and useful part is actually doing something with it.

The economics of this can be very good. If an Economy Plus seat would otherwise go unsold, giving it to an inconvenienced passenger costs United very little. The passenger gets something the airline normally charges for, and the message tells them why. Waiting until close to departure gives them more information about which seats they’re likely to sell. But an unannounced benefit delivered after booking can’t persuade someone to make that booking in the first place. A credit or an advance offer of a better seat can give an angry customer a reason to try the airline again. This gesture reaches people who already have another United reservation. And that doesn’t mean they’ve forgiven the airline. Their next trip could have been purchased before the bad trip. United may have the only convenient nonstop. They may be flying because their employer booked it. I especially like, though, that this can reach someone without status. An empty extra legroom seat may do more to win that customer’s business than offering the same thing to a frequent flyer who already gets it regularly. And United has to get the seat choice right. I wouldn’t consider moving from an aisle to a middle seat an improvement just because it’s in Economy Plus, and by the way United doesn’t offer free drinks in their extra legroom coach seats like even American does. Booking a table can be the least exciting part of a night out. However, the platform you use to do it can now earn you rewards worth anything from a few cents to a delicious discount on your bill.

OpenTable, DoorDash, Seated and now Resy all reward you for dining out, though each takes a different approach. OpenTable awards its own points, DoorDash issues credits for future orders, Seated offers rewards that can be redeemed for gift cards and Resy awards American Express Membership Rewards points.

As with your favorite coffee chain's loyalty program or a food delivery app subscription, the best option depends on where, how often and how much you eat out. Whichever you choose, you'll generally still earn rewards on eligible restaurant purchases when paying with a dining credit card, making your meal even sweeter.

In this guide, we compare what each program earns, what those rewards are worth and the fine print to watch so you can decide which one deserves a seat at your table.

*Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations.

Related: This overlooked dining program is one of the most generous and gets you $25 off your very first meal

OpenTable Regulars is free to join, and you'll earn 100 dining points for each reservation you book directly on OpenTable while signed in to your account and then complete. Reservations made through restaurant websites or third-party booking partners generally don't qualify. Points are posted only after you've dined, so canceled reservations and no-shows earn nothing.

Some restaurants in the program also offer bonus-point reservations worth 500, 750 or even 1,000 points at certain times. To find them, turn on the "bonus points filter" under special features in the OpenTable app.

Once you have at least 1,000 points, you can redeem them in the app's "Rewards" section at the following rates for U.S. members:

As for the redemption rate you'll get for each, they're:

That means a standard 100-point reservation is only worth 80 cents toward a future meal, and you'll need 20 of them to earn a $16 dining credit, which isn't very rewarding.

Dining credits work at participating OpenTable restaurants (look for the "Dining Credit Accepted" filter). After you redeem your points, you can add the credit to a reservation, which provides a digital Mastercard you can use toward eligible bills. Experience credits work similarly but only apply to certain prepaid experiences, such as prix-fixe menus and cocktail classes. Dining credits expire 12 months after you redeem them.

If you complete six reservations on OpenTable within 12 months, you'll then unlock Gold status for a year. Gold members get priority notifications when tables open up, a three-month complimentary Uber One trial for eligible new or returning members who do not have an active subscription and access to "Gold Tables," which promises harder-to-book tables at more than 500 participating restaurants in over 50 U.S. cities.

OpenTable also partners with Chase, Uber and Visa. Uber One members can book Uber One Exclusive Tables, eligible Visa cardholders can access tables and special events through the Visa Dining Collection and select Chase cardholders get exclusive tables and statement credits (more on that below).

Make sure you're actually turning up for your bookings, though. OpenTable will close your Regulars account and cancel all your points if you record four no-shows within 12 months. Your points also expire after 12 months of inactivity or after 3 years from the date you earn them, whichever comes first.

Related: Earn even more rewards when dining out with OpenTable

DoorDash is best known for delivery, but reservations are now available in select cities across the U.S., Australia and Canada. Its current market page lists 17 U.S. cities, plus Melbourne and Sydney in Australia and Toronto and Vancouver in Canada.

Rather than earn points, you earn promotional DoorDash credits when you book and complete an eligible reservation in the DoorDash app or on its website. The amount is shown before you book and now varies by restaurant, reservation time and membership status. Current U.S. listings commonly advertise $5 in credits, while some times display $10 or $12. Not every reservation earns a credit.

Credits are posted after you've paid for your meal and can be used toward eligible future DoorDash delivery or pickup orders. They typically can't be used to pay for taxes, fees or tips, expire six months after they're issued unless the offer says otherwise, have no cash value and can't be used to buy gift cards or alcohol.

Since the reward is a fixed amount, you don't earn more rewards for a higher food bill. A $5 credit is a 5% return on a $100 dinner but about 1.7% on a $300 tasting menu. A $10 credit would deliver returns of 10% and about 3.3%, respectively. That makes DoorDash Reservations especially appealing for smaller restaurant bills if you already use DoorDash.

DashPass members can earn more on eligible reservations, plus access exclusive prime-time tables and discounts on Lyft Black rides. However, the elevated reservation reward is no longer a simple fixed $2 boost across every listing, so check the offer shown before booking rather than assuming your membership guarantees a particular amount.

Check the restaurant's cancellation policy when you book. Late cancellations and no-shows may incur fees set by the restaurant, and DoorDash says excessive no-shows can result in suspension of your access to reservations.

Outside its reservation cities, DoorDash's "Going Out" tab also lists in-store offers at certain restaurants, with DashPass members earning extra rewards for repeat visits in some locations.

Related: Your complete guide to Chase and DoorDash

What is unique about this program is that you don't need to book through Seated: You link an eligible credit or debit card, then tap to activate the restaurants where you want to earn a higher reward rate before paying with your linked card. Eligible rewards then post automatically, with no receipts to upload.

Activations last until the end of the calendar month, and you can activate up to 25 restaurants per month (plus any monthly specials). Seated's app also advertises 5% back at participating restaurants, even without an activation, provided you open the app at least once every 30 days. Higher reward rates generally require activation, so it's worth activating your favorites at the start of each month and checking the offer terms in the app.

Rewards vary by restaurant but can be up to a generous 35% back, with the rate shown on each restaurant's page before you choose to activate it. Rewards are calculated on your eligible food-and-beverage total before tax and tip, so a restaurant offering 10% back would earn you $10 in Seated rewards on a $100 meal. Since each diner earns on the share they pay with their own linked card, splitting the bill doesn't cost anyone their individual rewards.

Seated partners with more than 2,500 restaurants in certain U.S. markets. Availability varies by city and neighborhood, so check the app for participating locations and current rewards before dining, rather than relying on a fixed city list.

You can then redeem Seated rewards for gift cards in the app's store tab, with available brands to choose from including Airbnb, Amazon, Dunkin', Nordstrom, Sephora, Starbucks, Target and Uber. Because rewards can then be converted to eligible gift cards at face value, TPG values them at $1 per $1 redeemed, provided you choose a brand you'd spend with anyway and meet any minimum redemption requirement.

The catch is that Seated rewards may expire after more than 30 days without qualifying account activity, so check the app's activity and expiration rules rather than assuming opening it alone preserves your balance. Seated also says its rewards can't be combined with other restaurant promotions, third-party deals (such as those available through Groupon) or discount offers.

If you're a new member, keep an eye out for a first-meal bonus offer of up to $10 through an eligible referral link or promotional offer, though this is not guaranteed for every member.

Related: Rove adds dining and in-store rewards in major platform expansion

Resy Rewards takes a different approach than the other three programs. It does not issue a stand-alone Resy currency. Instead, eligible U.S. American Express cardmembers earn 4 additional Membership Rewards points per dollar spent at participating restaurants, on top of the points their enrolled card already earns.

To participate, you must first enroll an eligible U.S. Amex card that earns Membership Rewards points in the Rewards tab of the Resy iOS app.

You must then book a participating restaurant through the Rewards tab, complete the meal and pay with the enrolled card. Merely dining at a participating restaurant or booking it through another part of Resy will not trigger the 4 bonus points per dollar. At launch, the program is only available through the Resy iOS app, meaning Android users cannot currently use it.

The initial New York City list includes restaurants like Carne Mare, Le Crocodile, Hearth, Kiko, Opto and Le Pavillon. American Express plans to expand Resy Rewards to additional U.S. cities and select Tock venues in 2027.

On a $100 eligible restaurant purchase, Resy Rewards would provide 400 bonus Membership Rewards points. Based on our valuation of 2 cents per Membership Rewards point, that is an estimated $8 in value (or an 8% return) before accounting for the card's standard earning rate.

Related: Don't overlook Resy: How to maximize dining experiences and save money with this Amex benefit

Because OpenTable and DoorDash reward reservations with a fixed amount while Seated pays a percentage of your bill and Resy pays a fixed number of points per dollar spent, the best option depends on how much you spend. Here's a comparison for $100 in food-and-drink purchases (before tax and tip), assuming the advertised offers apply and you can use the full value of the DoorDash credits on a later order:

If you spend $200 on a meal rather than $100, the OpenTable and DoorDash rewards stay the same, while the Seated rewards as a percentage of spending will quickly increase. Resy would also double to 800 bonus points, worth an estimated $16 with TPG's valuation of Amex points.

Seated can be the most rewarding option for larger restaurant bills, especially at restaurants that offer higher reward rates. However, its value depends on the percentage offered. DoorDash's fixed credits may still provide you with a better return on smaller bills or at restaurants that offer lower Seated rewards. Resy provides a consistent 8% estimated return from its bonus points — but only at its small number of participating restaurants at launch.

Related: The dining statement credits that save me over $1,000 every year

Certain restaurant purchases can also earn credit card rewards in addition to the benefits provided by these platforms. Combining these apps with a card that earns bonus points at restaurants can be an easy way to double-dip and earn more rewards. Some of the best options currently available include:

But it gets even better. Savvy diners keen on maximizing their rewards may be able to triple-dip by booking an eligible Sapphire Reserve Exclusive Tables restaurant through OpenTable and paying with their Sapphire Reserve card. Doing so will allow you to earn OpenTable Regulars points plus 3 Chase Ultimate Rewards points per dollar spent on the eligible dining purchase, even if you later receive a statement credit. Qualifying purchases at participating restaurants can also trigger the separate Sapphire Reserve dining credit, worth up to $150 per half-year.

Related: How to double-, triple- or even quadruple-dip on dining rewards

Resy Rewards offers a strong, straightforward points return at participating restaurants. However, the program is launching at only a handful of New York City restaurants and is available through the Resy iOS app, so most diners will not be able to use it regularly yet.

Seated has the highest potential return for larger dining bills. A restaurant offering 15% back would earn you $30 in rewards redeemable for gift cards on a $200 dinner, while a 35% offer would earn $70. Know, though, that higher rates generally require monthly activation, and you'll need to keep your rewards account active.

DoorDash Reservations can still be the best option for smaller meals when the booking carries a strong credit. A $10 or $12 reward can beat percentage-based programs on a modest check. The catch is that rewards now vary by reservation, availability is limited to select cities and the credits are less useful if you rarely order through DoorDash.

OpenTable Regulars is the least rewarding of the four for most standard reservations, with a 100-point booking worth just 80 cents at the best U.S. redemption rate. Still, it is the most broadly available of the four in the markets where its Dining Points program operates and offers useful extras, including bonus-point tables, Gold Tables and a three-month Uber One trial for eligible Gold members. Select Chase cardholders can also receive statement credits at eligible restaurants.

There's no single best dining rewards platform for everyone, as the right choice depends on where you live, how much you spend and how often you dine out.

Resy offers a compelling points return at participating venues, but its limited launch footprint and lack of an Android app make it more of a promising option than an everyday solution right now.

Seated can deliver the biggest reward on an expensive meal, while DoorDash can be particularly rewarding on a smaller bill when the booking offers a decent credit.

As for OpenTable, it remains the most broadly available of the four in the markets where its Dining Points program operates. Its nationwide coverage, Gold perks and Chase partnership make it worth considering, especially when you travel.

Since all four cost nothing to join, you may as well sign up for them all so you are ready the next time you want to book a meal. Just remember to show up for reservations or cancel within the restaurant's deadline, as no-shows can cost you points, credits or even access.

That's some food for thought before your next night out.

#6046. Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

Collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.

Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.

The amount of earmarks King secured fell dramatically compared to his previous year's total in Senate Appropriations Committee bills, as Collins took sole credit for most earmarks both senators had requested.

The power play has instigated a dispute over how to award credit for "congressionally directed spending," better known as earmarks. It has also raised questions about a Senate rule that requires committee leaders to disclose the name of each senator who requested projects to be included in a spending bill before it can move on the floor.

It’s undeniable that as the chair of the spending panel, Collins has more influence over which projects reach the final bills than her delegation mate. Collins spokesperson Phoebe Keller said that since available earmark funding is split into separate pots for the majority and minority to dole out, the bills reflect which of those funding sources was tapped to provide money to the relevant projects.

Keller said that Collins deserves sole credit for the contested projects, as listed in the reports accompanying the bills.

"When only Collins is listed, it reflects only she chose to fund the project,” Keller said.

A Democratic committee aide contested that characterization, saying that traditionally all requesters are named regardless of which party’s funding allocation is tapped for a project.

“The handling of these particular projects is a clear departure from the norm and will need to be rectified in conference negotiations,” the aide said.

King is credited with approximately $54 million in fiscal 2027 earmarks in the bills Collins released this month, including joint projects with Collins. That's down from around $231 million in the Senate's fiscal 2026 bills, according to a CQ Roll Call analysis.

Last year, King and Collins were both listed on 75 of the 77 projects that both requested that were included in the Senate bills, with just two carrying only Collins’ name. This year, Collins claimed sole responsibility for over $125 million in projects that both she and King requested, approximately two-thirds of the joint requests.

While King’s overall requests fell by more than $200 million this year versus last, his success in securing requested funds plummeted at a far greater rate with less credit for overlapping projects.

The joint requests for which Collins claimed sole credit include five for the Maine Department of Transportation in the Transportation-HUD bill, including $10.7 million for northern freight rail improvements; $9.6 million for Route 26 reconstruction in Oxford; and $7.2 million for improvements in Rockport, among others.

In the Labor-HHS-Education bill, projects Collins took sole credit for include $4 million for the University of Maine for biology laboratory equipment and just over $4 million for the creation of a modern emergency helipad at Lincoln Hospital.

And the Interior-Environment bill features $4 million each for wastewater improvements in Limestone and Kennebec that both Collins and King asked for but are only attributed to Collins, among others.

Similarly, the Agriculture, Commerce-Justice-Science and Homeland Security bills all include a project requested by both senators that only Collins is listed as securing in the bill.

The outgoing Appropriations chair’s ability to fuel billions of dollars in federal funding for her state during her career was the centerpiece of her ultimately unsuccessful campaign for reelection, which she lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.

As written, the draft bills appear to risk running afoul of a Senate rule that requires the committee’s chair to identify each senator who requested projects in a bill online at least 48 hours before a vote to advance the legislation on the floor.

The relevant rule, Senate Rule 44, states that it is out of order to vote on a motion to proceed to consider a bill unless the chairman of the committee certifies that “each congressionally directed spending item . . . has been identified through lists, charts, or other similar means including the name of each Senator who submitted a request to the committee for each item so identified.”

That information must be “available on a publicly accessible congressional website in a searchable format at least 48 hours before such vote.”

A King spokesman called on the spending panel to add his name to the relevant requests.

“We believe this must have been an oversight and assume the committee will update the requests —per Senate rules — once it’s called to their attention,” King spokesman Matthew Felling said.

The bills released by Collins are drafts, and no floor action on final fiscal 2027 spending bills is expected this Congress. There’s limited time left before the Dec. 11 spending deadline, when all current funding is set to expire, and Democrats want to wait to negotiate final bills until they retake majorities in both chambers next year.

But to comply with the rule, before the bills reach the floor the reports accompanying the bills, that includes the earmark tables, may have to be rewritten to list King on the contested projects, or the committee may need to disclose the information elsewhere online.

Both chambers unveiled stricter ethics guidelines surrounding earmarks in 2021 when the practice returned after a decade-long ban.

#6045. Grand Theft Auto VI and How We Spend Our Time

Your time on earth, no matter how long, is shorter than you think. Do you want to spend it doing chores in a simulated environment?

A gamer plays Grand Theft Auto VI during an unofficial launch party at OS Gaming Lounge in New York City on November 19, 2026.

Donald Trump just met with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China for a tripartite global summit — and nobody has any real news to report, except for Trump, so desperate for media attention that he’s giving interviews to anyone holding a hot mic and a video camera. The lack of news is not just because of a (predictable) blackout enforced by the Chinese Communist Party, but because the collective consciousness of America has shut down for the next few days. If you thought the traditional four-day Thanksgiving Day Weekend was typically slow, get ready for a one-and-a-half-week productivity dip in the economy as the video game Grand Theft Auto VI goes live across the nation. Even National Review, as sober-minded as it is, has more than a few fans of the series on its staff.

Every periodical you might care to read — even the political or news-based ones — has brought forward its big-think “review” of the game, now available on PlayStation and Xbox. For all I know we’ll be publishing one too. But I am not a gamer — not in the modern sense of the word, although I did whip out my copy of Battletoads for the NES the other day to prove that I’ve still “got it” — and this will not be a review of GTA VI. Instead, I want to talk about time spent — and time wasted.

A gamer plays Grand Theft Auto VI during an unofficial launch party at OS Gaming Lounge in New York City on November 19, 2026.

Jeffrey Blehar is a National Review staff writer living in Chicago. He is also the co-host of National Review’s Political Beats podcast, which explores the great music of the modern era with guests from the political world happy to find something non-political to talk about.

#6044. Delta’s CEO Says It Flew To LaGuardia In The 1950s—It Didn’t, But His Predecessors Figured Out How To Win New York

Delta CEO Ed Bastian says flying from Atlanta to LaGuardia takes longer today than when Delta launched the route in the 1950s. Except Delta didn’t fly to LaGuardia in the 1950s. Delta’s New York service began at Newark. It took another 13 years to start LaGuardia. And the distinction between serving New York and serving the airport a New Yorker actually wants has been costing airlines money ever since. Speaking with Fortune, Bastian said: Today it takes more time to fly from Atlanta to LaGuardia than it did in the 1950s when we first launched that flight, which is absurd. Delta’s history gives its LaGuardia launch date as October 1, 1969. Northeast and Northwest Airlines, which Delta later absorbed, served LaGuardia in 1945. But there was no Delta Atlanta–LaGuardia service in the 1950s. The airline that became such a powerful force in New York was a late arrival, built through acquisitions, deals with competitors, and an understanding of what New Yorkers would put in their wallets. The Mayor Who Refused To Get Off His Plane In New Jersey On November 24, 1934, New York Mayor Fiorello La Guardia arrived from Chicago on TWA. The plane landed at Newark. The mayor refused to get off. His ticket said New York. This was New Jersey. After an argument, the aircraft took him onward to Floyd Bennett Field in Brooklyn. He told the New York Times, “my ticket says New York and that’s where they brought me.” He repeated the stunt the following month. He wasn’t demanding to be taken to what’s now New York LaGuardia. That airport wouldn’t open until 1939. He was promoting New York City’s existing airport in Brooklyn, trying to pull airline business across the state line. Ironically, Floyd Bennett Field was about the same distance from Times Square as Newark. Delta’s First New York Flights Landed At Newark Delta didn’t grow up as a New York airline. Its roots were in Southern crop dusting, and its headquarters moved to Atlanta in 1941. Eastern had a substantial head start in the New York–Atlanta market. Back then an airline couldn’t just decide to add a route. The federal government’s Civil Aeronautics Board decided who could fly where. Delta’s 1956 annual report says its new route award allowed three daily round trips between New York and Newark. The launch timetable shows flight 724 leaving Atlanta at 6:05 p.m. and arriving at Newark at 9:21 p.m., with a Washington stop. That’s 3 hours 16 minutes. Comparing that one-stop propeller service with today’s nonstop wouldn’t tell us much about air traffic control in any case… Delta was already selling New York from Manhattan ticket offices, including Rockefeller Plaza. It added Idlewild, today’s JFK, on May 15, 1957. The airline’s August 1957 timetable shows Delta’s four-engine Flying Scot daytime coach flights using Idlewild, while its other flights used Newark. Why Did LaGuardia Take Until 1969? Delta had arrived late in a regulated market, and LaGuardia was difficult to get into. Eastern and American each essentially had a concourse to themselves, while the other airlines shared the remaining two. Delta initially served the airport with relatively small DC-9s, while Eastern already had 727s. Delta began advertising LaGuardia in its August 1969 timetable, Flight 620 will begin operating upon completion of arrangements for terminal facilities at LaGuardia. The actual October 1969 launch schedule offered non-stop service, not available from Delta’s 1950s service. Flight Leaves Atlanta Arrives LaGuardia Scheduled time 168 6:15 a.m. 8:15 a.m. 2 hours 620 12:10 p.m. 2:08 p.m. 1 hour 58 minutes 622 6:15 p.m. 8:13 p.m. 1 hour 58 minutes The 1956 annual report advertised a future Atlanta–New York time of 1 hour 41 minutes aboard forthcoming DC-8 jets, which Delta hadn’t introduced yet. How Delta Bought Its Way Into Being A New York Airline A Civil Aeronautics Board examiner recommended giving Delta New York–Miami authority in 1956, but the board itself rejected that awarding the service to Northeast. Sixteen years later, Delta bought Northeast. That 1972 acquisition brought a much stronger position in New York, Boston and Florida. In 1991, Delta acquired Pan Am’s transatlantic operation and its Northeast shuttle. Then came the deal that changed the scale of LaGuardia. Proposed in 2009 and completed in 2011, the US Airways slot swap gave Delta 132 daily LaGuardia slot pairs. US Airways received 42 daily Washington National pairs, $66.5 million, and rights for additional São Paulo service. The Government Accountability Office measured Delta’s LaGuardia slot share rising from 24% in April 2011 to 44% in May 2012. Regulators required slots to go to smaller competitors as a condition of approval. At LaGuardia, JetBlue received eight daily pairs and WestJet another eight. JetBlue actually bid the most for both packages, but the auction rules wouldn’t let one airline win both. Then, as I reported in 2024, following Enilria’s examination of slot trades, Delta even managed to get back the eight round trips WestJet had received as a competition remedy. Slots handed to a rival to keep Delta’s expansion competitive wound up back with Delta. US Airways helped Delta grow at LaGuardia. United would help at JFK. When United pulled out in 2015, Delta took over its JFK slots under a long-term lease. Delta also spent money leveraging that access with its $4 billion LaGuardia terminal project. United Tried To Prove Newark Was New York Using Taxi Ads Newark is a New York metropolitan airport. Depending on where you’re going and the traffic, it can be the most convenient one. It also serves a large and wealthy New Jersey market in its own right. United’s digital taxi top campaign showed real-time driving estimates to Newark and JFK. The advertising industry’s account reveals the best detail: when Newark wasn’t the quickest, the display switched to generic United branding. The comparison disappeared when United lost it. When United left JFK in 2015, that meant premium Los Angeles and San Francisco service to Newark. After Scott Kirby joined United, he called the decision a mistake. The airline had looked at the money its JFK flights made or lost. Kirby explained that leaving also helped American win corporate accounts such as Disney and Time Warner. Those customers bought travel beyond Los Angeles–New York, including Los Angeles–London. United returned to JFK in 2021, then left again in 2022 after failing to obtain the access it wanted to build a larger operation. Its Blue Sky partnership with JetBlue provides another way back: access for up to seven daily United round trips from JFK’s new Terminal 6 as early as 2027, alongside reciprocal loyalty benefits and the ability to sell each other’s flights. Winning New York Also Means Winning Credit Card Spending I’ve made the same argument about American’s retreat in major markets. An airline needs to be useful where high-spending customers live. Otherwise why would those customers choose its credit card? A New Yorker who wants LaGuardia for domestic trips and JFK for longer journeys is a candidate for a Delta Amex (even though those miles are worth less than competing currencies). Delta’s investor presentation connects large coastal metropolitan economies with its premium and loyalty growth. In 2023 Delta described its cobrand spending as approaching 1% of U.S. GDP. Using American Express’s disclosures for that year—Delta represented about 10% of $1.680 trillion in worldwide network volume—implies roughly $168 billion. Against the contemporary $27.36 trillion estimate of U.S. GDP, that’s about 0.61%. As I’ve argued, they’re rounding generously. And there’s a bigger problem with the growth story. When Delta renewed its American Express deal in 2019, it projected $7 billion annually by 2023. It delivered $6.8 billion. That sounds like nearly hitting the target, until you account for how much pandemic-era inflation had shrunk the value of each dollar – in a way that hadn’t been anticipated in 2019. Consumer prices rose about 19% between 2019 and 2023. Using annual consumer price indexes, the $6.8 billion payment had only about $5.7 billion of 2019 purchasing power. Delta nearly hit its 2019 goals in nominal terms due to inflation, but its actual performance was a real miss. Delta now expects more than $9 billion from American Express in 2026. It’s an enormous business, but it’s had a ceiling greater than what Delta had hoped in 2019 – which also explains the importance of free wifi, Uber and Starbucks – looking for new customers anywhere they can find them. The poor return on spending of a Delta credit card finally matters. Ultimately, though, Delta wasn’t born a New York airline. Ed Bastian’s predecessors assembled one, including airport access its competitors willingly gave up. United is still working to repair its decision to leave JFK. For customers who insist that their New York ticket take them to a particular New York airport, being told Newark is close enough still doesn’t close the sale. And Bastian’s 1950s comparison is typical Bastian – never let facts like connecting service and which airport the airline served get in the way of the story he wants to tell. Delta’s New York service began at Newark. It took another 13 years to start LaGuardia. And the distinction between serving New York and serving the airport a New Yorker actually wants has been costing airlines money ever since.

Today it takes more time to fly from Atlanta to LaGuardia than it did in the 1950s when we first launched that flight, which is absurd.

Delta’s history gives its LaGuardia launch date as October 1, 1969. Northeast and Northwest Airlines, which Delta later absorbed, served LaGuardia in 1945. But there was no Delta Atlanta–LaGuardia service in the 1950s.

The airline that became such a powerful force in New York was a late arrival, built through acquisitions, deals with competitors, and an understanding of what New Yorkers would put in their wallets.

On November 24, 1934, New York Mayor Fiorello La Guardia arrived from Chicago on TWA. The plane landed at Newark. The mayor refused to get off. His ticket said New York. This was New Jersey. After an argument, the aircraft took him onward to Floyd Bennett Field in Brooklyn. He told the New York Times, “my ticket says New York and that’s where they brought me.” He repeated the stunt the following month. He wasn’t demanding to be taken to what’s now New York LaGuardia. That airport wouldn’t open until 1939. He was promoting New York City’s existing airport in Brooklyn, trying to pull airline business across the state line. When United pulled out in 2015, Delta took over its JFK slots under a long-term lease. Delta also spent money leveraging that access with its $4 billion LaGuardia terminal project. United Tried To Prove Newark Was New York Using Taxi Ads Newark is a New York metropolitan airport. Depending on where you’re going and the traffic, it can be the most convenient one. It also serves a large and wealthy New Jersey market in its own right. United’s digital taxi top campaign showed real-time driving estimates to Newark and JFK. The advertising industry’s account reveals the best detail: when Newark wasn’t the quickest, the display switched to generic United branding. The comparison disappeared when United lost it. When United left JFK in 2015, that meant premium Los Angeles and San Francisco service to Newark. After Scott Kirby joined United, he called the decision a mistake. The airline had looked at the money its JFK flights made or lost. Kirby explained that leaving also helped American win corporate accounts such as Disney and Time Warner. Those customers bought travel beyond Los Angeles–New York, including Los Angeles–London. United returned to JFK in 2021, then left again in 2022 after failing to obtain the access it wanted to build a larger operation. Its Blue Sky partnership with JetBlue provides another way back: access for up to seven daily United round trips from JFK’s new Terminal 6 as early as 2027, alongside reciprocal loyalty benefits and the ability to sell each other’s flights. Winning New York Also Means Winning Credit Card Spending I’ve made the same argument about American’s retreat in major markets. An airline needs to be useful where high-spending customers live. Otherwise why would those customers choose its credit card? A New Yorker who wants LaGuardia for domestic trips and JFK for longer journeys is a candidate for a Delta Amex (even though those miles are worth less than competing currencies). Delta’s investor presentation connects large coastal metropolitan economies with its premium and loyalty growth. In 2023 Delta described its cobrand spending as approaching 1% of U.S. GDP. Using American Express’s disclosures for that year—Delta represented about 10% of $1.680 trillion in worldwide network volume—implies roughly $168 billion. Against the contemporary $27.36 trillion estimate of U.S. GDP, that’s about 0.61%. As I’ve argued, they’re rounding generously. And there’s a bigger problem with the growth story. When Delta renewed its American Express deal in 2019, it projected $7 billion annually by 2023. It delivered $6.8 billion. That sounds like nearly hitting the target, until you account for how much pandemic-era inflation had shrunk the value of each dollar – in a way that hadn’t been anticipated in 2019. Consumer prices rose about 19% between 2019 and 2023. Using annual consumer price indexes, the $6.8 billion payment had only about $5.7 billion of 2019 purchasing power. Delta nearly hit its 2019 goals in nominal terms due to inflation, but its actual performance was a real miss. Delta now expects more than $9 billion from American Express in 2026. It’s an enormous business, but it’s had a ceiling greater than what Delta had hoped in 2019 – which also explains the importance of free wifi, Uber and Starbucks – looking for new customers anywhere they can find them. The poor return on spending of a Delta credit card finally matters. Ultimately, though, Delta wasn’t born a New York airline. Ed Bastian’s predecessors assembled one, including airport access its competitors willingly gave up. United is still working to repair its decision to leave JFK. For customers who insist that their New York ticket take them to a particular New York airport, being told Newark is close enough still doesn’t close the sale. And Bastian’s 1950s comparison is typical Bastian – never let facts like connecting service and which airport the airline served get in the way of the story he wants to tell. A Civil Aeronautics Board examiner recommended giving Delta New York–Miami authority in 1956, but the board itself rejected that awarding the service to Northeast. Sixteen years later, Delta bought Northeast.

That 1972 acquisition brought a much stronger position in New York, Boston and Florida. In 1991, Delta acquired Pan Am’s transatlantic operation and its Northeast shuttle.

Then came the deal that changed the scale of LaGuardia. Proposed in 2009 and completed in 2011, the US Airways slot swap gave Delta 132 daily LaGuardia slot pairs. US Airways received 42 daily Washington National pairs, $66.5 million, and rights for additional São Paulo service. The Government Accountability Office measured Delta’s LaGuardia slot share rising from 24% in April 2011 to 44% in May 2012.

Regulators required slots to go to smaller competitors as a condition of approval. At LaGuardia, JetBlue received eight daily pairs and WestJet another eight. JetBlue actually bid the most for both packages, but the auction rules wouldn’t let one airline win both.

Then, as I reported in 2024, following Enilria’s examination of slot trades, Delta even managed to get back the eight round trips WestJet had received as a competition remedy. Slots handed to a rival to keep Delta’s expansion competitive wound up back with Delta.

Ed acts like he ascended the ranks of…a soda company before becoming an airline CEO.

Ironically, AA WAS a NYC airline but has managed to squander that and is now just in third place even including EWR.

B6 is a true NYC airline but it keeps shrinking in the NE.

UA also bought its way into NYC w/ the CO merger so the two NYC powerhouses are “outsiders”

and, if credit card revenues could be publicly alloted to cities, DL’s NYC operation is very likely the most lucrative in the US. for an outsider and southerner, DL has played its cards in the NE and on the west coast very well.

Ah, back to the old “but, but… Newark is the ‘New York City’-area…” Fine, it is; and, depending on which part of town you’re heading, EWR is closer than JFK. Is Ed trying to pull one of those? How ironic because, well, you know, the Delta-United rivalry. Dead fanboys, get on here and feud some more!

American was a true NY airline, even headquartered there, until the wake of deregulation, when it decamped to Ft. Worth around 1980.

United was nearly irrelevant in the NY market until it merged with Continental. It had JFK transcons to LAX and SFO, one or two flights to IAD at JFK, and 3 daily to LHR, plus NRT and a short lived HKG route, a weekly CCS service at one point, a weekly SJU flight, and one daily to SEA. At LGA, it just had ORD, DEN, and IAD. United was Newark’s #2 airline for years in the 1980s and 1990s though and had a decent presence there, including LHR and NRT.

Delta was also never really that big in NY and principally a NY to Florida and Atlanta airline. The footprint got bigger with the 1991 acquisition of the shuttle and the JFK footprint from Pan Am, but for 15 years post that, DL really didn’t know what to do with NYC until it emerged from bankruptcy in 2007 and went on a construction tear and a campaign to win NY corporate business. It wisely took the LGA slots from an idiotic USAirways in exchange for DCA slots (USAirways was squatting on LGA slots with turboprops to Roanoke and Richmond and not places NY’ers want to go to. From that point on, DL won NY.

JetBlue is a NY airline, but it is shrinking itself into irrelevance and is so debt laden, it likely will go the Chapter 11 to Chapter 7 route in the next 18 months.

Newark is a New York Metropolian area airport; to say otherwise is special needs; unless one thinks Cincy has no air service since the airport is in Kentucky or New Orleans is out of luck since the airport is not in the city itself. Unless NYC is giving up the Jets and Giants to New Jersey also…it is amazing how 10,000s of people can go watch the Giants or Jets play football (ok maybe the Jets don’t play, per se) in North Jersey but somehow the same travel to EWR is somehow prohibitive. It is ridiculous and the numbers from the PA show as much.

#6042. Rove Gives You 1,500 Free Miles Just For Signing Up—Plus 5,000 More On Your First $500 Hotel Booking

Rove is offering 1,500 free miles just for signing up. You don’t have to book a trip, buy anything, or complete any other transaction. I specifically asked about an activity requirement, and Rove confirmed that new members get the miles instantly. I’ve written quite a bit about Rove, and asked them to improve the offer available through my link. This is three times the standard 500-mile referral signup bonus. Just like normal referrals, I receive Rove Miles when someone signs up through this link. It doesn’t cost you anything. In fact it gets you much more than not using this link. They’ve also created a hotel booking code for readers: 1,500 miles for joining: Use this link to create your new account. There’s no purchase requirement. 5,000 additional miles on your first hotel booking of $500 or more: Enter promo code VFTW when booking through Rove. A new member who uses both offers would earn 6,500 bonus miles, on top of the normal miles from their qualifying hotel booking. You can also just take the signup miles. And 5,000 miles on a $500 booking is twice what Rove offered at that spending level during its May promotion. What You Can Do With These Miles Rove is a free rewards program that lets you earn miles from hotel and flight bookings, online shopping, dining and gift cards. You don’t have to apply for a credit card, and you can earn rewards from the card you use to pay as well. Their transfer partners include familiar programs like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France KLM Flying Blue, Qatar Airways Privilege Club and Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. They also have programs that are harder to access through the major bank currencies, including Lufthansa Miles & More (for better availability of business and first class awards), Japan Airlines Mileage Bank (better availability of awards, lower prices on partner awards), Air India Maharaja Club (United awards starting at just 3,500 points) and Copa ConnectMiles (Emirates awards with no fuel surcharges). Rove has a 2,000-mile minimum for partner transfers. You don’t need a hotel stay to earn additional miles. I’ve covered Rove’s dining program and instant gift card rewards, and just wrote about its personalized shopping offers of up to 25 miles per dollar. When The Hotel Bonus Makes Sense You can also redeem Rove Miles directly for travel. As I wrote last month, I can usually get around 1.5 cents apiece redeeming them for hotel stays that still earn hotel points and elite status credit. Using that benchmark, the 5,000-mile hotel bonus is worth about $75 toward travel. On a qualifying $500 booking, that’s an extra 15% in value before the booking’s regular rewards. Expressed another way, the promo adds 10 miles per dollar at exactly $500 in qualifying spend. I’ve been particularly interested in Rove’s Loyalty Eligible hotel rates. There are two different kinds of bookings to compare: Loyalty Eligible rates generally earn 5 Rove miles per dollar, while preserving eligibility for the hotel’s own points, elite night credit and status benefits. The hotel charges your card, which can make paying with that chain’s credit card attractive. Rove Rates can offer more Rove miles, with the site advertising up to 25 per dollar, but generally give up the hotel loyalty program earnings and benefits. That tradeoff is easier at an independent hotel where you wouldn’t earn chain points anyway. I’d take the free signup miles. For the hotel offer, enter VFTW and consider the rate you’re selecting before booking for the 5,000-mile bonus. #6040. House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, says banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the new year.

But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the issue could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.

“I’d rather have it be a clean bill focused on stock trading, and not muddy it by adding other topics, even if they’re good policies,” said Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I.

The incoming majority could plant a flag on government accountability with a broad package ranging from insider trading to campaign finance and more. Or they could zoom in on the stocks issue with a standalone bill.

Magaziner said he hasn’t received any assurances from House Democratic leaders, instead describing a “collaborative conversation” about what form the legislation could take.

“I worry that it would get weighed down under its own weight if you try to load it up with too many things,” Magaziner said, while stressing he would support whatever expected incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries decides.

Meanwhile, more than half of the Democrats in the incoming freshman class are calling for action on Day One of the new Congress, sending a letter to Jeffries last week suggesting they make a “down payment on much-needed reform” by changing House rules to curb stock trading.

“Democrats may have won the election, but we have a long way to go to earn back the trust of voters across the country,” reads the letter, led by Reps.-elect Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa and Jamie Ager of North Carolina. “A stock trading ban alone will not fix Washington, but it is the fastest way to show voters we heard them.”

Folding new language into the House’s internal rules would be a relatively easy path, requiring just a majority vote on the House floor, instead of passage in both chambers and the president’s signature. But such internal limits wouldn’t have the force of law, and some believe it would cool the urgency around the issue while doing little to crack down on insider trading.

Colorado Rep. Jason Crow said moving forward quickly with a rule change wouldn’t preclude passing a bill, suggesting his fellow Democrats do both.

“I want to pursue a parallel track,” said Crow, who co-chairs the End Corruption Caucus. “We want to move via rule and just prohibit it right out of the gate, or as much as we can.”

Jeffries has repeatedly said the topic is high on his to-do list as he looks to deliver on the accountability the “American people are demanding.”

“We’re committed to making sure we pass legislation that bans members of Congress from trading stocks. That will be a high priority,” he said at a news conference this week.

But with more than two dozen different bills on the topic introduced over the past few years alone, lawmakers will have to decide exactly what a “ban” means to them.

Some want to force members of Congress to fully offload their stocks with the exception of widely held mutual funds. Other proposals would block lawmakers from buying new stocks but allow them to keep the ones they already own, like a Republican-led bill that passed the House earlier this year but stalled in the Senate.

Democrats resisted that push, which was led by outgoing House Administration Chair Bryan Steil, R-Wis., partly because it included an unrelated voter ID provision they called a “poison pill.” Many also complained the measure didn’t go far enough, extending to members’ spouses and dependent children but leaving out key figures in other branches of government, such as the president.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., said she wants to stay close to the text of a consensus bill she hammered out last year with a small bipartisan group that included Magaziner and Reps. Chip Roy, R-Texas, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa.

“That is the most comprehensive, thorough, thoughtful proposal and bipartisan proposal that we have,” she said of the bill, dubbed the Restore Trust in Congress Act.

That measure would not apply to President Donald Trump, as many Democrats have urged as they seek to draw attention to his ballooning wealth while in office. Still, Jayapal suggested a presidential stock trading ban could be moved separately.

“There is discussion about the president, vice president, Cabinet, Supreme Court. I know we’re working on some language around enforcement, around those pieces, but I actually think that can be a separate bill,” Jayapal said. “We want to hold everyone accountable — but at minimum, we have to do ourselves.”

It’s not clear how much appetite will exist next year for a bipartisan compromise that could realistically clear a 60-vote cloture threshold in the Senate. Notably, key Republicans who worked on the consensus bill will be leaving Congress, with Roy losing a primary bid for Texas attorney general and Fitzpatrick unseated by a Democratic challenger.

While lawmakers could in theory advance a new stock-trading bill even sooner, before Democrats take control of both chambers, time and patience is short in the lame-duck session.

At a news conference at the Capitol earlier this week with Crow and Jayapal, a group of freshman and returning Democrats took matters into their own hands, promising not to hold or trade individual stocks as part of a broader pledge backed by the Political Integrity Project.

“My district, New York 10, happens to include Wall Street, but I don’t represent Wall Street. I represent the people of Brooklyn and Manhattan who deserve someone who goes to work every single day and shows right up front, ‘I work for you.’ And what better way to prove that than by day one showing we will ban members of Congress from enriching themselves, from trading stocks?” Rep.-elect Brad Lander said.

While momentum has grown in recent years as key senior lawmakers softened their resistance to a stock trading bill, not everyone is on board. Some members still argue, whether publicly or privately, that they should be able to trade on the stock market just like other citizens or that existing disclosure requirements established by a 2012 law are already enough to discourage dubious trades.

As they iron out the legislative text of any new bill, members will have to decide how to handle emerging topics such as prediction markets and crypto, along with sticky questions such as whether to allow blind trusts. And extending restrictions to the president could be a nonstarter for many Republicans.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., said Democrats in the next Congress should look to a bipartisan bill that advanced out of the Senate Homeland and Governmental Affairs Committee in July 2025 as a model.

“The legislation we passed out of the committee applied to the executive branch,” he said. “But it didn’t take effect for anybody until their next terms, which was a compromise.”

That proposal would apply to future presidents but not the current one, potentially freeing up more Republicans to vote for it without angering Trump. Still, it hasn’t seen action on the Senate floor.

Hawley said that while he’d like to see a “full ban on trading and holding” in Congress, he would be open to a weaker proposal in the interest of getting something done.

“I’ll take anything that’s an incremental improvement over what we have now, which is nothing,” he said.

As much as I love the holiday season, it's my least favorite time to travel. Flights and accommodations are expensive, airports are at their busiest and winter storms can upend even the best-laid plans.

A credit card can't help your family pack lighter or ensure your flight departs on time. But the right benefits can lessen the sting from some of travel's most predictable pain points.

Here are the cards that can make the biggest difference during a hectic holiday trip, organized by the problem they solve.

Few travel fees are more annoying than paying extra to bring your socks with you — especially now that roundtrip bag fees can feel higher than the cost of the clothes inside.

For a family checking multiple bags, this may be the most immediately valuable benefit on this list. A card with a relatively modest annual fee can pay for itself during holiday travel alone.

Many airline credit cards offer a free checked bag, so start with the airline you fly most.

Higher-fee airline cards often match or exceed the checked-bag benefits shown here.

Many of the same airline cards that waive bag fees also provide priority boarding benefits. On a packed holiday flight, I'll gladly get in line early if it keeps my carry-on out of the gate-check pile.

The $895 annual fee (see rates and fees) offers another way to lower the cost of bags or boarding. Its up to $200 annual airline incidental credit can reimburse eligible expenses such as checked bag and seat selection fees with one selected qualifying airline (enrollment required). This is a useful way for existing cardmembers to absorb a holiday expense.

The (see rates and fees) offers a broader alternative: Its $300 annual travel credit applies automatically to eligible travel purchases, including checked bag fees.

Related: Which airline credit cards offer the best priority boarding perks?

Ever spend more time in airport security than you do on the flight itself? TSA PreCheck, Global Entry and Clear+ earn their keep throughout November and December.

PreCheck provides expedited screening at eligible U.S. airports; Global Entry includes PreCheck and adds expedited processing when returning to the U.S. from abroad; and Clear+ uses biometric identity verification to speed up the document-check step of security (so some travelers use it alongside PreCheck).

And for travelers who frequently cross between the U.S. and Canada, Nexus can speed up passport control.

I like this benefit because it works regardless of which airline you're flying and gives you something that's often in limited supply: time. Just apply well before your trip because Trusted Traveler applications take some time to process. You can't open a card on Monday and expect to breeze through security on Friday.

A lounge won't make a delayed flight leave sooner, but a power outlet, snacks and a drink make the wait easier.

These lounge cards offer different benefits:

* Up to 10 visits per eligible Platinum Card, per year to the Delta Sky Club or to Grab and Go when traveling on a same-day Delta-operated flight

I've had all of these over the years, although lately my favorite card for lounge access is the Bank of America Premium Rewards Elite. The card's Priority Pass membership still provides credits at participating airport restaurants, which can be helpful when traditional lounges are full or there's nowhere left to sit.

There's a broader lesson there, too: don't choose a card based solely on how many lounges its network advertises. Check whether your airports have participating locations, whether there are restrictions on when you can visit and if it costs extra to bring your travel companions.
